    All in One View

    Content from Welcome and the Story

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What will we do over these two half-days, and why?
    • What is the project we’ll be working on?

    Objectives

    • Explain what “curating history” means
    • Check your setup works
    • Meet peakfinder and your pair partner

    Welcome

    This workshop is about a habit more than a command:

    Leave a git trail that is easy to review, merge and understand.

    You already know how to make history. Over the next two half-days we’ll learn how to curate it: to shape the commits you leave behind so that the people who read them, including you in six months, can follow what happened and why.

    It is not a course on obscure git commands. It’s a course on how one working style, with a handful of tools, makes collaboration much easier. Along the way we’ll look inside git, because the tools make more sense when you know what git is doing.

    Why bother?

    Two versions of the same piece of work, as a git log. Take a moment to read them.

    Version A

    OUTPUT 

    d8cc138 readme
9e1626f try smoothing
4244130 fix typo
2b17bef cli stuff
9a6471e remove print
89f7c6f add tests
33aa1de fix
21dd6b4 tidy up
ead2b48 wip
cd6792e add background module

    Version B

    OUTPUT 

    b8f52dd Document --subtract-background in the README
e7fab65 Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
514955f Add tests for background subtraction
37e6d49 Add rolling minimum background subtraction
17f1b3d Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks
754c449 Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows
5fb3ed3 Handle constant spectra in normalise

    The two contain exactly the same code. Only the story is different.

    Challenge

    Discussion: which would you rather review?

    Vote (a show of hands in the room, or a reaction in the chat) for the one you’d rather review. Then, with the person next to you (or in the chat), say why. Think about:

    • Could you tell what each commit is for?
    • What if a bug turned up in one of the changes? Which log makes it easier to find, undo or copy somewhere else?
    • Which one tells you why the code changed, not just that it did?

    Nearly everyone picks B. In A, you can’t tell what wip, fix or tidy up mean without opening each commit. Some of the changes are unrelated to each other. And one commit, try smoothing, is an experiment that was abandoned.

    In B, every line says what the change is, and each change is separate. You can review them one at a time, revert one, or copy a single fix onto another branch.

    By the end of tomorrow, you’ll be able to turn A into B, and better, you’ll learn how to write B in the first place.

    The story

    Throughout the workshop we’ll work on a small Python package called peakfinder. It finds peaks in spectra: the bumps in a curve that tell you something about a sample. You’ll need no knowledge of spectroscopy. The code is deliberately short and plain.

    Try it, now. In your peakfinder clone (with your virtual environment active):

    BASH 

    python -m peakfinder.cli data/example_spectrum.csv | wc -l
python -m peakfinder.cli data/example_spectrum.csv --plot

    OUTPUT 

    71

    The program reports 71 “peaks”, but there are only three real ones. All the other bumps are noise. (If a plot window appears, you’ll see the three big peaks and a lot of little red dots. If no window opens, use --save-plot spectrum.png and open the file.)

    We have a job to do. We’re going to improve peakfinder, and we want to do it in a way our collaborators can follow.

    flowchart LR
    accTitle: {The story across the two days}
    accDescr: {Six steps in order. Day 1, shown in green: rescue a messy branch, then build your own feature with tidy commits. Day 2, shown in blue: a colleague's work lands first and you resolve the conflict, you find the change that caused a bug, you review each other's work and set up CI, and you release a fix.}
    A1["Day 1<br/>Rescue a<br/>messy branch"] --> A2["Day 1<br/>Build your own<br/>feature, tidily"]
    A2 --> B1["Day 2<br/>Colleague's work lands:<br/>resolve the conflict"]
    B1 --> B2["Day 2<br/>Find the change<br/>that caused a bug"]
    B2 --> B3["Day 2<br/>Review each other,<br/>set up CI"]
    B3 --> B4["Day 2<br/>Release<br/>a fix"]
    classDef day1 fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    classDef day2 fill:#def,stroke:#05a,color:#000
    class A1,A2 day1
    class B1,B2,B3,B4 day2
    • Day 1: you are the author. You’ll learn how git really works, how to plan changes, and how to rescue a messy branch. Then you’ll build a feature of your own, one tidy commit at a time.
    • Day 2: you are a collaborator. A colleague’s work lands on main while you were busy, so you’ll deal with the conflict. Then you’ll track down the change that caused a bug, review each other’s work, and release a fix.

    The plan for the two days

    • Day 1: making history. How git really works, planning and atomic commits, a safety net, shaping commits, rewriting a messy branch, and the daily loop that keeps history tidy.
    • Day 2: sharing and maintaining history. Rebase versus merge and conflicts, tracking down a bug, pull requests, catching problems early with CI, and releasing a fix.

    The episodes are listed in the sidebar. We’d rather go at a comfortable pace than cover everything. If we run short of time, we’ll skip things at the end, rather than rush.

    Work in pairs

    You’ll work in pairs. Your partner is the person who reviews your pull request on day 2, and who you can ask for help. You each work on your own computer and your own copy of the project.

    Online, we’ll put you in breakout rooms of two.

    Do this now, to save time tomorrow. Give your partner access to your fork:

    1. On GitHub, open your fork of peakfinder, then Settings, then Collaborators, then Add people.
    2. Enter your partner’s GitHub username.
    3. Your partner will get an email invitation, and should accept it. (You can also accept at https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/peakfinder/invitations, using your own username.)

    Do it in both directions, so you each have access to the other’s fork.

    Quick check before we start

    Please check the following. Put a hand up (or message the helpers) if any of them is a problem:

    Ground rules

    • Ask questions at any time. If something looks odd, it probably is, and someone else is wondering too.
    • Help your partner, but let them type. People learn from doing.
    • Nothing here is permanent. We’ll be breaking things deliberately, and git almost always lets us get back. We’ll learn how in episode 4.
    • We follow The Carpentries Code of Conduct.

    Timing. 10 minutes talking, 5 for the discussion. If the setup check turns up problems, give helpers the stragglers and keep going. Don’t let the whole room wait for one laptop.

    The hook. Put the two logs up side by side. Don’t tell people which is “right”. Let them say it. Then say “The code is identical.” That is the idea of the whole workshop.

    Noisy plot. Make sure everyone has seen the 71. In episode 7 they’ll write a feature to fix it, and it helps them to care.

    Collaborator invitations. This is where people get stuck: the invitation sits in an email, and the invitee must accept. Check that pairs have done it now. On day 2, PR review needs it.

    Common setup problems (see the setup page for fixes):

    • forked with “Copy the main branch only” ticked (so only main, no tags): delete the fork and fork again
    • no way to git push (authentication)
    • core.editor not set, so the rebase editor will be vim
    • virtual environment not active, so pytest is not found

    Online. Drop the list of pairs in the chat, and create the breakout rooms before they’re needed. Have a helper in every room if possible.

    Pairs with an odd number. A trio works: one person is the reviewer for the next.

    Key Points
    • This workshop is about curating history: leaving commits that are easy to review, merge and understand
    • The same code can have a confusing history or a clear one, and the clear one is far easier to work with
    • Day 1 is about producing good history, and day 2 is about sharing and maintaining it
    • You’ll work in pairs, and your partner reviews your pull request

    Content from A Mental Model: Snapshots and Labels

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 22 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is a commit, really?
    • What are branches and HEAD?
    • Why does “rewriting history” create new commits, rather than editing old ones?

    Objectives

    • Describe a commit as a snapshot that points to its parent
    • Explain why changing a commit changes its hash, and the hashes of everything after it
    • Explain branches and HEAD as labels that point at commits
    • Use this model to predict what a command will do

    Why bother?

    You already use git every day without knowing what is inside it, and that’s fine. But in this workshop we will be changing history, and it’s much less scary if you know what git is actually doing. We need just four ideas.

    Idea 1: a commit is a snapshot

    You have probably heard that a commit is “a set of changes”. That is a useful way to think about it, and we will use it too. But it is not what git stores.

    Git stores a snapshot of your whole project at that moment, along with a message, an author, and a pointer to the previous commit (the parent).

    Let’s look inside a real one. In your peakfinder clone, first list the latest commits. The top one is the commit that HEAD is on, which means “where you are now”:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline -3

    Now print the commit object for that commit. This is the commit as git stores it:

    BASH 

    git cat-file -p HEAD

    OUTPUT 

    tree 82fa2f38d5d1864f890ecd4ef923bafbb8e65985
parent b7cf029bfa65c05266bfce11a30c889f9e36378d
author Sam Scientist <sam.scientist@example.org> 1736175600 +0000
committer Sam Scientist <sam.scientist@example.org> 1736175600 +0000

Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks

    That is all a commit is: a small piece of text. (cat-file -p prints a git object, and here the object is the commit at HEAD.) Three things are worth noticing:

    • tree is the hash of another git object (a tree), which stores a snapshot of every file in the project at this point in time. We won’t go any deeper than that.
    • parent is the hash of another commit: the one that came before. Look back at your git log output and you’ll find it just below.
    • The rest is the author, date and message.

    Here is the part that matters. A commit’s hash is (essentially) a hash of this text. You can check:

    BASH 

    git rev-parse HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD | git hash-object -t commit --stdin

    OUTPUT 

    1e81f2713978c508941a5b8366aabd892b635104
1e81f2713978c508941a5b8366aabd892b635104

    The same hash, twice. (git log --oneline only shows the first 7 characters.) Keep this in mind, as the text includes the parent’s hash, and we’ll see in a moment why that matters.

    So where is the “change”? It isn’t there. When you run git show or git diff, git works out the differences between two snapshots on the spot.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Commits are snapshots that point to their parent}
    accDescr: {Three commits, C1, C2 and C3, drawn left to right. Each is a snapshot of the whole project. Each has an arrow pointing back to the commit before it, which is its parent.}
    C3["C3<br/>snapshot"] -->|parent| C2["C2<br/>snapshot"]
    C2 -->|parent| C1["C1<br/>snapshot"]

    Notice that the arrows point backwards, from each commit to its parent. That’s how git stores it: a commit knows its parent, but it doesn’t know its children. So in all the diagrams from here on, time runs from left to right: the oldest commit is on the left, and the arrows point back towards it.

    Callout

    So is a commit a snapshot or a diff?

    Both ideas are useful, a bit like light being a wave and a particle.

    • When you review, cherry-pick or write a commit message, think of a commit as a change (a diff).
    • When you ask “what does the project look like at this commit?”, or you wonder how rebase works, think of it as a snapshot.

    We will tell you which one we mean when it matters.

    Idea 2: hashes chain commits together

    Every commit has an ID, like 1e81f27. It’s called a hash, and it’s calculated from the contents of the commit, including the parent’s hash.

    This has an important consequence:

    If you change anything about a commit, it gets a new hash. And then its child has a different parent, so the child gets a new hash too, and so on all the way to the tip of the branch.

    Before:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Four commits in a chain}
    accDescr: {Four commits, C1 to C4. Each points back to the one before it.}
    C4 --> C3 --> C2 --> C1

    After changing C2:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {The same chain after C2 is changed}
    accDescr: {C1 is unchanged. C2 has been changed, so it is a new commit, C2 prime. C3 and C4 now point at new parents, so they are new commits too, C3 prime and C4 prime. The new commits are marked in green.}
    C4p["C4'"] --> C3p["C3'"] --> C2p["C2'"] --> C1
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class C2p,C3p,C4p new

    Green marks commits that are new. Everything after the change gets a new hash.

    There is no such thing as editing a commit in git. You can only make a new, similar commit. This is exactly why rewriting history is a thing you have to do carefully.

    Try it. Make a scratch branch and change the message of the latest commit:

    BASH 

    git switch -c scratch
git log --oneline -1
git commit --amend -m "A different message"
git log --oneline -1

    OUTPUT 

    1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks
...
c91e7a2 A different message

    The hash is different. (Yours will be, too, as it also depends on the time you did it.)

    Idea 3: old commits don’t disappear

    So what happened to 1e81f27? Ask git for it:

    BASH 

    git show 1e81f27 --stat

    It’s still there, and still intact. Nothing points to it from scratch any more, but git hasn’t deleted it. Git keeps a private diary of where HEAD has been, called the reflog, and we’ll use it in episode 4 to get back to commits like this one. It’s why we can be relaxed about trying risky things in episode 6.

    (The commit stays until git’s garbage collection removes unreachable commits, which only happens after a few weeks.)

    Idea 4: branches and HEAD are labels

    If commits never change, how does a branch “move” when you add a commit?

    A branch is a label (a name) that points at one commit. It’s a tiny file containing a hash:

    BASH 

    cat .git/refs/heads/scratch
git log --oneline -1

    When you commit, git makes the new commit and moves the label forward to it.

    HEAD is also a label: it says “where you are now”. Usually it points at a branch, which points to a commit:

    BASH 

    cat .git/HEAD

    OUTPUT 

    ref: refs/heads/scratch
    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {HEAD points at a branch, which points at a commit}
    accDescr: {HEAD points to the branch called scratch. The scratch branch points to commit C3. C3 points back to C2, which points back to C1.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> scratch(["scratch"]) --> C3
    C3 --> C2 --> C1

    Now add a commit and the label moves:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After a new commit, the branch label moves forward}
    accDescr: {HEAD still points to the scratch branch, but scratch now points to the new commit C4. C4 points back to C3, then C2, then C1.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> scratch(["scratch"]) --> C4
    C4 --> C3 --> C2 --> C1

    git switch moves HEAD to a different label. git branch name sticks a new label on the current commit. Making and deleting branches is cheap because a label is all they are.

    Callout

    What is “detached HEAD”?

    It’s HEAD pointing at a commit directly, instead of at a branch. You get it if you check out an old commit, and git warns you about it. It isn’t a problem. It simply means that if you commit now, no branch label will move to follow you. We’ll use it deliberately in the bisect episode.

    Clean up your scratch branch:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git branch -D scratch
    Challenge

    Knowledge check: where are the labels?

    You don’t need to type anything for this one. Start from here:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Starting point: main is at C3 and HEAD is on main}
    accDescr: {Three commits, C1, C2 and C3. The branch main points at C3, and HEAD points at main.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> main(["main"]) --> C3
    C3 --> C2 --> C1

    Now these commands are run, one after the other. (--allow-empty just lets us make commits without changing any files.)

    BASH 

    git switch -c feature
git commit --allow-empty -m "C4"
git commit --allow-empty -m "C5"
git switch main
git commit --allow-empty -m "C6"

    On paper, or in your head: where do main, feature and HEAD point at the end? Which label moved at each step?

    Step by step, the labels move like this. (Green marks commits that are new.)

    After git switch -c feature: nothing moved except HEAD. A new label was stuck on C3.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After switching to a new branch called feature}
    accDescr: {Nothing has moved except HEAD. The new branch feature points at C3, the same commit as main, and HEAD now points at feature.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> feature(["feature"]) --> C3
    main(["main"]) --> C3
    C3 --> C2 --> C1

    After the two commits (C4, C5): each commit moved the label HEAD was on, feature, forwards. main stayed where it was.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After two commits on feature}
    accDescr: {Two new commits, C4 and C5, shown in green, sit on top of C3. The feature branch has moved forward to C5, and HEAD is still on feature. Main has not moved: it is still at C3.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> feature(["feature"]) --> C5
    C5 --> C4 --> C3
    main(["main"]) --> C3
    C3 --> C2 --> C1
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class C4,C5 new

    After git switch main and the commit C6: switching moved only HEAD. Then C6 moved main. The history has diverged from C3.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After switching back to main and making a commit}
    accDescr: {The history has diverged from C3. Feature points at C5, on a line C4 then C5. A new commit C6, shown in green, sits on top of C3 on a second line, and main points at it. HEAD is now on main.}
    HEAD(["HEAD"]) --> main(["main"]) --> C6
    feature(["feature"]) --> C5 --> C4 --> C3
    C6 --> C3
    C3 --> C2 --> C1
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class C6 new

    So at the end feature is at C5, and main and HEAD are at C6. We’ll see two ways to bring the two lines together in episode 9.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: new hash or not?

    Which of these gives the commit a new hash?

    1. Fixing a typo in its message
    2. Moving the branch label to a different commit
    3. Changing the commit that comes before it
    1. Yes: the message is part of the commit’s contents.
    2. No: the commit isn’t changed, only the label.
    3. Yes: the parent is part of its contents, so the hash changes as well.

    Keep this brisk (about 25 minutes). The goal is a useful model, not a complete one, and people may ask about trees, blobs or packfiles. Park those and point them at the extras. If you want a deeper treatment (optional, end of day 2, or the learner reference), the deep dive is: objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags), content addressing, git hash-object, .git/objects.

    Likely questions:

    • “So git doesn’t store diffs?” Conceptually it stores snapshots. Under the hood it is clever about storing them compactly (packfiles), but you don’t need to care.
    • “What if two commits have the same content?” Different parents or timestamps mean different hashes.
    • “Can I see the old commit later?” Yes, that’s the next-but-one episode (reflog).
    Key Points
    • A commit is a snapshot of the project plus a pointer to its parent. Diffs are worked out when needed
    • A commit’s hash depends on its contents and its parent, so changing one commit changes all those after it
    • You can’t edit a commit, only make a new one. The old one is still there
    • Branches and HEAD are just labels pointing at commits. Committing moves the label

    Content from Planning and Atomic Commits

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 23 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I plan a change before I start typing?
    • What makes a commit easy to review?
    • What should a commit message say?

    Objectives

    • Sketch a commit plan for a small change
    • Describe an atomic commit
    • Write a commit message with a short subject and a body that says why
    • Spot a commit that mixes unrelated changes

    Why history matters

    Think about the last time you looked back through a project’s history. You might have been:

    • trying to work out why a line is the way it is
    • hunting for when something broke
    • reviewing a colleague’s changes
    • copying a fix onto another branch

    Every one of those jobs is easier if the history was written for a reader. Everything else in this workshop is a tool for doing that. First we need to know what we are aiming at.

    Plan the work, then the commits

    Most people start a piece of work by opening a file and typing. Try this instead. Before you write any code, spend a couple of minutes on two questions.

    1. What is the overall change you want to make?

    Say it in one sentence, and say what “done” looks like. For example:

    “Peaks that are lower than a minimum height should be ignored, because our example data reports 71 peaks when only three are real.”

    If it takes a paragraph, or a lot of “and”s, the change is probably too big for one branch. Split it up now.

    2. What changes are needed along the way?

    List the steps it takes to get there. Any step that can stand on its own is a candidate for a commit. For the example above:

    1. Add a min_height option to find_peaks
2. Add tests for min_height
3. Add a --min-height option to the command line

    That list is your commit plan. It:

    • tells you whether the change is small enough. If you’ve written ten steps, the work should probably be split into two branches.
    • gives each step a name before you’ve started, which makes the commit message easy later
    • helps you notice what’s missing, like the tests or the command line
    Callout

    The plan is a guess

    You will get it wrong, and that is fine. You might find a bug that has to be fixed first, or realise step 2 should come before step 1. Update the plan and carry on. We’ll cover how to put commits in the right order after the fact, so a wrong plan costs you very little.

    The point isn’t to follow the plan exactly. It’s to stop yourself producing one giant lump of work.

    If you’ve come across them, this is the same instinct as slicing a big task into small stories in an agile team: the smaller the piece, the easier it is to plan, do and review.

    What is an atomic commit?

    An atomic commit is one complete, logical change. It:

    • does one thing, so you can describe it in one sentence without using “and”
    • leaves the project working: the tests pass at that commit, not just at the end of the branch
    • can be understood on its own, and could be undone or copied elsewhere without dragging other changes along

    “Atomic” doesn’t mean “tiny”. A commit that adds a function and its tests can be perfectly atomic. A one-line commit that fixes a bug and renames a variable is not.

    Not atomic:   "Fix normalise and add background subtraction and update README"
Atomic:       "Handle constant spectra in normalise"
              "Add rolling minimum background subtraction"
              "Document --subtract-background in the README"

    Why bother?

    These commits pay off throughout the workshop, and long after:

    When you… atomic commits mean…
    review a branch’s pull request you can read one idea at a time
    revert a mistake you can undo just the bad bit
    cherry-pick a fix onto a release you can take the fix and nothing else (episode 13)
    bisect to find a bug the commit that introduced a problem is one small commit, not a large lump (episode 10)
    Callout

    An example: keep the refactor apart from the change

    Imagine you need to change what a function returns, and the code is in an awkward place, so you also move it into a new file and reorganise it as you go. Here is the same work as one commit, and as two:

    As one commit, the reviewer can’t tell what was moved and what was changed, so they have to read all of it as if it were new code. As two commits, the first is a pure refactor they can skim, check the tests still pass, and move on. The second is a small diff about the one thing that really changed. They can trust that the first commit is boring, and spend their attention on the second.

    Callout

    We’re not being obsessed

    Nobody will mind if a commit is slightly more or less than one thing. The aim is that a reviewer can follow your reasoning. When you’re not sure, ask: if this commit turns out to be wrong, would I want to throw away all of it?

    A good commit message

    Here is a message from the peakfinder history:

    Add mode option to normalise

Adds 'max' and 'area' modes alongside the default 'range'.

    A good message has:

    1. A subject line: short (about 50 characters), in the imperative mood, as if giving an order. “Add”, “Fix”, “Remove”, not “Added” or “Adds”. A handy test: “If applied, this commit will … [subject]”.
    2. A blank line.
    3. An optional body, for anything the subject can’t say. Explain why, because the diff already shows what.

    Most commits need only a subject. Use the body when the reason isn’t obvious from the code:

    Handle constant spectra in normalise

A flat spectrum has max equal to min, so we were dividing by zero.
Return zeros instead.

    Compare these:

    Weak Better
    fix Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero
    updates Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows
    wip (something you’d fix before sharing, see episode 6)
    Callout

    Optional: commit message prefixes

    Some projects start every subject line with a short tag that says what kind of change it is. This makes a long git log easier to scan, and it can be used to build a changelog automatically. There are two common styles:

    Kind of change Scientific Python style (NumPy, pandas) Conventional Commits
    New feature ENH: feat:
    Bug fix BUG: fix:
    Tests TST: test:
    Documentation DOC: docs:
    Refactor (no behaviour change) MAINT: or REF: refactor:
    Formatting, style STY: style: 
    ENH: Add min_height option to find_peaks
BUG: Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero

    Neither is “right”, and many projects use no prefix at all. If your project has a convention, follow it. If not, it’s up to you and your team, and it’s more important to be consistent than to pick the best one. We won’t use prefixes in the workshop examples.

    There is a bonus: a prefix is an atomicity check. If you can’t choose just one, such as BUG: or REF:, you have probably got two commits.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: atomic or not?

    Which of these would you be happy to see as a single commit?

    1. “Add min_height option to find_peaks, with tests”
    2. “Fix bug in normalise, rename y to intensity everywhere, update README”
    3. “Remove unused import from cli.py”
    4. “Many changes”
    1. Yes. The feature and its tests are one logical change.
    2. No. Three unrelated changes. A reviewer has to untangle them, and if the rename causes trouble you can’t undo it without undoing the bug fix.
    3. Yes. Small, but it is complete and has a clear purpose.
    4. No. It says nothing about what, or why.
    Challenge

    Challenge: spot the smells, and make a plan

    You have been working on background subtraction for a week, and you’re about to ask for a review. Take a look at your branch:

    BASH 

    git switch background-subtraction
git log --reverse --stat --format='%h %s' main..

    OUTPUT 

    cd6792e add background module
 peakfinder/background.py | 8 ++++++++
ead2b48 wip
 peakfinder/background.py | 9 ++++++++-
21dd6b4 tidy up
 peakfinder/io.py        | 6 +++---
 peakfinder/normalise.py | 5 ++++-
 peakfinder/peaks.py     | 2 ++
 tests/test_normalise.py | 4 ++++
 tests/test_peaks.py     | 7 +++++++
33aa1de fix
 peakfinder/background.py | 4 ++--
...

    (Use the arrow keys to scroll, and q to quit.)

    Work with the person next to you, and don’t run any more git commands that change things. Just read, and answer:

    1. Which commits have messages that tell you nothing?
    2. Which commit mixes unrelated changes? How can you tell?
    3. Which commits are really corrections to an earlier commit, or shouldn’t be in the history at all?
    4. Write down the list of commits you wish the branch contained. In episode 6 you’ll turn this branch into your list.

    Tip: git show <hash> shows what a commit actually changed, and the Source Control view and Timeline in VS Code are another way of browsing it.

    1. wip, tidy up, fix, cli stuff, fix typo, readme, add tests and add background module all say little or nothing about the change.
    2. tidy up. It touches five files and does three unrelated things: a fix in normalise, a change to load_spectrum, and a new check in find_peaks. The stat shows several files that have nothing to do with each other, and the vague message hides it.
    3. wip, fix, remove print and fix typo all correct or finish the add background module commit. And try smoothing adds an experiment (scratch_smoothing.py) that nothing uses.
    4. One sensible plan:
      1. Handle constant spectra in normalise
      2. Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows
      3. Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks
      4. Add rolling minimum background subtraction
      5. Add tests for background subtraction
      6. Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
      7. Document --subtract-background in the README
      Yours might be slightly different (for example, you may fold the tests into commit 4), and that is OK as long as you can explain it.

    That gap, between the branch you have and the list you wish you had, is what episode 6 closes.

    Timing: about 15 minutes of talk and 10 for the challenge. The challenge is reading only, in pairs, and we reuse the plan in episode 6. Keep it light: don’t spend long on commit message conventions, people have strong opinions and it is a rabbit hole. Show the table of “weak vs better” and move on.

    Possible discussion points:

    • “Should tests go in the same commit as the code?” There are two schools of thought. Our view: yes, if a commit changes behaviour, the test for it belongs with it, so every commit stands alone. But a separate test commit is fine, and our messy branch has one.
    • “This is too much work.” Answer: you will write less time worth of commit message than you save in review. And episodes 5 to 7 show how to get there without planning perfectly.
    • “What about squash merging? Doesn’t that make this pointless?” Squash is a good fallback when a branch has not been curated, but it throws away exactly the story we’re trying to tell. We’ll come back to this in episode 9.

    Make sure everyone writes the plan down (a text file or paper). They’ll need it in episode 6.

    Key Points
    • Plan your commits before you start: a short list keeps each change small
    • An atomic commit does one logical thing and leaves the project working
    • A commit message has a short imperative subject, and a body that says why when it isn’t obvious
    • Atomic commits make review, revert, cherry-pick and bisect much easier

    Content from The Safety Net: Reflog

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I undo a mistake in git?
    • Can I really lose work?

    Objectives

    • Read the reflog
    • Recover from a bad git reset --hard
    • Bring back a deleted branch
    • Know what the reflog can’t save

    Why now?

    From the next episode on we will be changing history: amending, resetting and rebasing. If that sounds risky, this episode is the reason it isn’t. Git keeps a private diary of where you’ve been, and it can get you back.

    Remember from episode 2: when you “change” a commit, git makes a new one and moves a label. The old commit is still there, but nothing points at it any more. The reflog is how you find it again.

    What is the reflog?

    Every time HEAD moves (when you commit, switch branch, reset, rebase, merge…) git writes a line in a log. See yours:

    BASH 

    git reflog

    OUTPUT 

    1e81f27 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from experiment to main
fba8092 HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to HEAD@{1}
1e81f27 HEAD@{2}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
fba8092 HEAD@{3}: commit: Note gaussian fitting idea in README
1634522 HEAD@{4}: commit: Note smoothing idea in README
...

    (Use q to leave the pager.) Yours will look different, as it’s a record of your actions.

    Each line says: the commit HEAD pointed to, HEAD@{n} (that position, counting back from now), and what you did to get there. The newest entry is at the top.

    The reflog is:

    • local: it lives in your clone and is never pushed. Your colleagues have their own.
    • temporary: entries expire. By default after 90 days, or 30 days if the commit is no longer on any branch.
    • only about commits. Remember that last point, we’ll come back to it.

    Oh no: a bad reset

    Let’s make some work and then destroy it. Follow along with the instructor, and type each step yourself. Make a throwaway branch and two commits:

    BASH 

    git switch -c experiment
echo "- Idea: smooth the spectrum before peak finding" >> README.md
git commit -am "Note smoothing idea in README"
echo "- Idea: fit gaussians to the peaks" >> README.md
git commit -am "Note gaussian fitting idea in README"
git log --oneline -3

    OUTPUT 

    fba8092 Note gaussian fitting idea in README
1634522 Note smoothing idea in README
1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks

    Now the mistake. You meant to undo one commit, but you typed a 2 and also added --hard:

    BASH 

    git reset --hard HEAD~2

    OUTPUT 

    HEAD is now at 1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks

    Both commits seem to be gone, and the lines have vanished from README.md. (We’ll explain exactly what reset does in the next episode. For now: it moved the branch label back two commits and threw away the changes.)

    Don’t panic. Look at the reflog. (The hashes in our examples will be different from yours, because they depend on the time you made the commits. Always use the ones on your screen.)

    BASH 

    git reflog

    OUTPUT 

    1e81f27 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
fba8092 HEAD@{1}: commit: Note gaussian fitting idea in README
1634522 HEAD@{2}: commit: Note smoothing idea in README
1e81f27 HEAD@{3}: checkout: moving from main to experiment
...

    The line fba8092 HEAD@{1}: commit: Note gaussian fitting idea in README is where we were before the reset.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After a reset, the commits still exist and the reflog remembers them}
    accDescr: {A chain of three commits, C1, C2 and C3. After the reset the branch experiment points at C1, so C2 and C3 are shown dashed because nothing points at them. The reflog, shown as a dotted note, remembers that HEAD was at C3.}
    experiment(["experiment<br/>(after the reset)"]) --> C1
    C2 --> C1
    C3 --> C2
    reflog[/"reflog remembers:<br/>HEAD was at C3"/] -.-> C3
    classDef orphan stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class C2,C3 orphan

    Dashed commits still exist, but no branch points at them. The reflog is how you find your way back to one.

    Move the branch label back there:

    BASH 

    git reset --hard fba8092

    OUTPUT 

    HEAD is now at fba8092 Note gaussian fitting idea in README

    Both commits are back, and so is the file’s content.

    Callout

    Use the hash, not HEAD@{n}

    You can write git reset --hard HEAD@{1}, and it often works. But the numbers shift every time HEAD moves, including when you run the recovery commands. Read the reflog and copy the hash of the line you want. It never changes.

    Callout

    A quicker undo: ORIG_HEAD

    Before risky commands such as reset, merge and rebase, git remembers where you were in ORIG_HEAD. So straight after a mistake, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD often puts you back. The reflog covers the cases where you’ve done other things since.

    Oh no: a deleted branch

    Delete the branch (we have to switch away first, and -D forces deletion of unmerged work):

    BASH 

    git switch main
git branch -D experiment

    OUTPUT 

    Deleted branch experiment (was fba8092).

    Look: git even tells you the hash. If you missed that, the reflog still has it:

    BASH 

    git reflog

    Find the last commit of the branch (the line that says commit: Note gaussian fitting idea in README) and make a new label there:

    BASH 

    git branch experiment fba8092
git log --oneline experiment -3

    The branch is back, with both commits. Now tidy up:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git branch -D experiment

    What the reflog can’t save

    The reflog records commits. Work that was never committed isn’t in it:

    • Edits you made and never committed, then threw away with git restore . or git reset --hard: gone.
    • Edits you staged but never committed: usually gone too (technically git may keep the content, but finding it is painful).
    • Anything older than the expiry time.
    • Commits only ever made on someone else’s computer.

    The rule that follows: commit before you try something risky. Even a messy “wip” commit, which we know how to tidy up afterwards. A commit can be recovered, and an uncommitted edit cannot.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: can I get it back?

    For each situation, can you get the work back? How?

    1. You committed three times on a branch, then ran git reset --hard main.
    2. You edited peaks.py, never committed, and ran git restore peaks.py.
    3. You ran git branch -D feature before it was merged.
    4. You did an interactive rebase last week and now realise you dropped a commit you needed.
    1. Yes. Find the last of the three commits in git reflog and git reset --hard <hash>.
    2. No. The changes were never committed, so git has no record of them.
    3. Yes. git branch -D prints the hash of the tip, and the reflog has it too: git branch feature <hash>.
    4. Yes, as long as it’s within the expiry (90 days / 30 days). The reflog shows where the branch was before the rebase. Look for the rebase (start) entry and the one before it. This is why we’ll be relaxed about rebasing.

    Pacing. This episode is the follow-along: learners type every step with you, so go slowly and pause after each command until people have caught up. There’s no separate challenge. If someone falls behind, they can watch and catch up at the knowledge check.

    Do the “oh no” moments as a live demo with everyone following. The drama is the point: say “I’ve lost all my work!” and pause before looking at the reflog.

    Cleanup: make sure everyone ends the episode with main checked out, and with a clean git status. A bad README.md change left on main would cause confusing conflicts later. If anyone committed to main by mistake: git reset --hard origin/main (they have a fork, so it will be at the right place).

    VS Code has no built-in reflog view. (The GitLens extension adds one.) This is a terminal job.

    Common problems:

    • The reflog opens in a pager and people don’t know how to leave. It’s q.
    • Someone runs git reset --hard with uncommitted work, and asks about it. Use it as the live demonstration of “what the reflog can’t save”.
    Key Points
    • Git rarely deletes commits straight away. The reflog records where HEAD has been, so you can find them
    • Recover by copying the hash from git reflog and using git reset --hard <hash> or git branch <name> <hash>
    • The reflog is local and expires, and doesn’t cover uncommitted work
    • Commit before trying something risky

    Content from Shaping a Commit: Staging, Amend, Reset and Restore

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 27 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I commit only part of my changes?
    • How do I fix the commit I just made?
    • What do reset and restore do?

    Objectives

    • Stage individual hunks and lines using the VS Code Source Control view
    • Amend the last commit, to change its message or add to it
    • Describe what git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard each move
    • Discard or unstage changes with git restore

    The staging area is a drafting table

    You know the three places a change can be:

    flowchart LR
    accTitle: {Where a change lives: working files, staging area and repository}
    accDescr: {Three boxes from left to right. Changes start in your working files. Staging moves them to the staging area, which holds the next commit. Committing moves them to the repository. Unstaging moves a change back from the staging area to the working files.}
    W["Working files<br/>(what is on disk)"] -->|"stage<br/>(git add)"| S["Staging area<br/>(the next commit)"]
    S -->|"git commit"| R["Repository<br/>(committed history)"]
    S -.->|"unstage<br/>(git restore --staged)"| W

    The staging area (also called the index) is where you assemble the next commit. It’s the feature that makes atomic commits possible: you don’t have to commit everything you changed. You choose.

    Most beginners stage whole files. But often one file contains two ideas. You can stage parts of a file as well.

    Staging parts of a file in VS Code

    Open the Source Control view: click the branch icon in the left sidebar, or press Ctrl+Shift+G (Cmd+Shift+G on a Mac).

    Every changed file is listed. Click one, and VS Code shows a side-by-side diff: the old version on the left and your working copy on the right.

    Now you can stage part of it:

    1. Select some lines in the diff, on the right-hand side. Click and drag, or click one line.
    2. Right-click and choose Stage Selected Ranges.

    Only those lines go into the staging area. The file now appears in both lists: Staged Changes has the part you picked, and Changes has the rest.

    You can also:

    • Use the Stage and Revert buttons in the gutter of the diff editor (next to your selection or a change), to stage or revert just those lines, or a whole block (a hunk), in one click.

    Commit as usual: type the message in the box at the top of the Source Control view and press Ctrl+Enter.

    Changed your mind? Unstage versus discard

    These two sound alike, and they are very different:

    I want to… VS Code Command
    Unstage: keep my edits, but leave them out of the next commit click the - icon, or select lines and Unstage Selected Ranges git restore --staged <file>
    Discard: throw my edits away, for good right-click the file, Discard Changes (or select lines and Revert Selected Ranges) git restore <file>

    Unstaging is always safe. Discarding isn’t: uncommitted edits aren’t in the reflog (episode 4), so there’s no way back. (Older guides use git checkout -- <file> and git reset <file> for these. They do the same thing, but restore has a clearer name.)

    Callout

    The command line version: git add -p

    You may see this in documentation, or need it over ssh where there is no VS Code:

    BASH 

    git add -p peakfinder/plot.py

    Git shows one hunk at a time and asks what to do:

    OUTPUT 

    @@ -2,22 +2,24 @@ ...
-def draw(ax, x, y, peaks):
+def draw(ax, x, y, peaks, title=None):
...
(1/1) Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]?
    Key Meaning
    y stage this hunk
    n don’t stage it
    s split it into smaller hunks
    e edit the hunk by hand
    q quit
    ? help

    It does the same thing as the VS Code view. Use whichever you find clearer. We’ll use VS Code in this workshop, because you can see the whole file and the context while you decide.

    Fixing the last commit: amend

    You’ve just committed, and you notice a typo in the message. Or you forgot to include a file. Instead of making a “fix typo” commit, you can amend the last one.

    VS Code:

    • To change the message or to add more changes: stage what you want to add, then open the dropdown arrow on the Commit button and choose Commit (Amend). (The same thing is under the ... menu, then Commit, then Commit Staged (Amend).)

    Command line:

    BASH 

    git commit --amend                  # change the message (opens your editor)
git commit --amend --no-edit        # add staged changes, keep the message

    Remember episode 2: the amended commit is a new commit with a new hash. The old one is still in the reflog. So only amend commits you haven’t shared with anyone. (Amend only works on the last commit. For an earlier one, you’ll use --fixup and interactive rebase, in episodes 6 and 7.)

    Moving where you are: reset

    git reset moves the branch label (and HEAD with it) to another commit. We saw in episode 2 that a branch is just a label, so this is simple to picture.

    Before:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Before the reset: main points at C4}
    accDescr: {Four commits, C1 to C4. The branch main points at C4.}
    main(["main"]) --> C4 --> C3 --> C2 --> C1

    After git reset HEAD~2:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After git reset HEAD~2: main points at C2}
    accDescr: {The branch main now points at C2. Commits C3 and C4 still exist, shown with dashed outlines, but nothing points at them.}
    main(["main"]) --> C2 --> C1
    C4 --> C3 --> C2
    classDef orphan stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class C3,C4 orphan

    Dashed commits still exist, but no branch points at them. Older commits are on the left.

    What happens to your files? That depends on the mode:

    Command Branch label Staging area Working files
    git reset --soft <commit> moves kept (the undone changes stay staged) kept
    git reset --mixed <commit> (the default) moves reset (the undone changes are unstaged) kept
    git reset --hard <commit> moves reset reset: your changes are lost

    In plain words:

    • soft: “undo the commit, but keep all the changes ready to commit again”
    • mixed: “undo the commit, and keep the changes, but I’ll choose what to stage again”
    • hard: “throw it all away” (the dangerous one)

    You’ll use mixed all the time in this workshop. It means: take this commit apart so I can build it again, better.

    Resetting in VS Code

    VS Code doesn’t have a button for each mode, but you can build all three from its buttons. Start from the Source Control view:

    You want Click Same as
    soft: undo the last commit, keep the changes staged ... menu, Commit, Undo Last Commit git reset --soft HEAD^
    mixed: undo the last commit, keep the changes unstaged Undo Last Commit, then Unstage All Changes (the - next to Staged Changes) git reset HEAD^
    hard: undo the last commit and throw its changes away Undo Last Commit, then Discard Changes on each file (right-click a file under Changes, it asks you to confirm) git reset --hard HEAD^

    (Undo Last Commit and Discard Changes are in VS Code’s own documentation. The buttons that act on a whole list at once, such as Unstage All Changes, appear when you hover over the Staged Changes header.)

    Resetting on the command line

    The commands in the table above are all you need: add HEAD^ (or HEAD~1, “the commit before this one”) to go back one commit, or HEAD~3 to go back three. Unlike the buttons, the command line can move the branch to any commit (git reset --hard <hash>, as we did in episode 4).

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: which reset?

    Which mode would you use if you wanted to:

    1. Undo your last commit but keep every change staged, so you can fix the message and recommit?
    2. Undo your last commit and unstage everything, so you can split it into two commits?
    3. Throw away your last commit and all the work in it? (Think carefully!)
    1. --soft
    2. --mixed (the default)
    3. --hard. Only if you’re sure! If you aren’t, commit the work to a new branch first, or remember that the reflog can find the commit again (episode 4).
    Challenge

    Challenge: untangle a commit

    It’s the end of a long day, and you have committed everything in one go. Your branch untangle has a single commit, badly named plot stuff. It contains three different things:

    1. A new feature: a --title option so you can put a title on the plot (changes in cli.py and plot.py)
    2. A small fix: the red peak markers were hiding behind the line, so they’re now drawn on top (one line in plot.py)
    3. A leftover debug print in cli.py that should never be committed

    Your job is to turn it into two clean commits, with the debug print gone:

    1. Add --title option for the plot
    2. Draw peak markers on top of the line

    Steps:

    1. Switch to the branch and look at the commit.

      BASH 

      git switch untangle
git show --stat

    2. Take the commit apart so the changes are in your working files, but not staged. (Which reset mode? Which buttons?)

    3. Use the Source Control view to stage only the title feature, and commit it.

    4. Stage the marker fix and commit it.

    5. Discard the debug print.

    Check your work:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline -3
git show --stat HEAD~1
git show --stat HEAD
git grep DEBUG
pytest
python -m peakfinder.cli data/example_spectrum.csv --save-plot title.png --title "Example"

    You should see two new commits, the first touching cli.py and plot.py, the second only plot.py. git grep DEBUG should print nothing, the tests should pass, and title.png should have a title.

    Hints:

    • In the diff editor, select a range of lines and use Stage Selected Ranges. You don’t have to stage whole files.
    • The title feature is spread over several places in both files. The easiest way to find them all: the lines that mention title.
    • Anything you leave unstaged stays in your working files, so it’s easy to do things in the right order.

    Take the commit apart. A mixed reset keeps the changes in your files but unstages them. In VS Code, click ..., Commit, Undo Last Commit. The changes appear under Staged Changes, so click Unstage All Changes. (Or in the terminal:)

    BASH 

    git reset HEAD^
git status --short

    OUTPUT 

     M peakfinder/cli.py
 M peakfinder/plot.py

    Commit 1: the feature. In the Source Control view, open cli.py. In the diff, select the line parser.add_argument("--title", ...), right-click, Stage Selected Ranges. Do the same for the two changes that pass title=args.title to plot_spectrum. Don’t stage the line starting print("DEBUG".

    Open plot.py. Stage every change that mentions title: the extra parameter on draw, the if title: lines, the extra parameter on plot_spectrum, and both calls to draw. Don’t stage the one line with zorder=3.

    Type the message Add --title option for the plot and press Ctrl+Enter.

    Commit 2: the fix. plot.py now only has the zorder=3 line left. Stage the file (click the +), and commit it as Draw peak markers on top of the line.

    Discard the debug print. cli.py has one change left, the DEBUG print. Click Discard Changes next to it.

    Command line version (for reference):

    BASH 

    git add -p peakfinder/cli.py       # answer: s, y, n, y
git add -p peakfinder/plot.py      # answer: s, y, n, y, y, y, y
git commit -m "Add --title option for the plot"

git add peakfinder/plot.py
git commit -m "Draw peak markers on top of the line"

git restore peakfinder/cli.py

    The s splits a big hunk up, and the n in the middle skips the zorder change in plot.py. In cli.py it skips the debug print.

    Demo first (about 5 minutes). Do the first hunk of the challenge live in VS Code, so people see Stage Selected Ranges working: undo the commit, stage the lines about --title in cli.py, and show the file in both the Staged and the Changes lists. Then leave the rest to them.

    Things that go wrong:

    • “Stage Selected Ranges” is greyed out. They selected lines in the left (old) side of the diff or nothing at all. It has to be the right-hand side.
    • They stage the whole file by clicking +. They can unstage it again with -, or Unstage Selected Ranges for a part.
    • They commit the debug print and then need to remove it. Fine: it’s a chance to show git commit --amend, or git reset HEAD^ and again.
    • They discard something they wanted with Revert Selected Ranges. If it was committed, the reflog has it. If not, it’s gone. Use it as a reminder of episode 4.
    • VS Code shows no ... menu or Amend option: an older VS Code. Use the command line.

    Don’t skip the debrief (3 minutes). Ask: “How did you decide which lines go in which commit?” The answer, “by the idea they belong to”, is the skill.

    The untangle branch is built by tools/build_starter.py, and is the same for everyone.

    Key Points
    • The staging area lets you assemble a commit. Stage hunks or individual lines in VS Code (or with git add -p)
    • git commit --amend replaces the last commit, so only do it for commits you haven’t shared
    • git reset moves the branch label: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them
    • git restore discards edits or unstages files without moving any label

    Content from Interactive Rebase: Rewriting a Messy Branch

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 43 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I reword, reorder, combine, split and drop commits?
    • What does git rebase actually do to my commits?

    Objectives

    • Run git rebase -i and use pick, reword, drop, fixup and edit
    • Reorder commits by moving lines in the todo list
    • Split one commit into several
    • Explain what rebase does in terms of snapshots and new commits
    • Back out of a rebase with git rebase --abort

    Where we left off

    For the last week you have been adding background subtraction to peakfinder, and you’ve just been told the work is ready for review. Take a look at your branch:

    BASH 

    git switch background-subtraction
git log --oneline main..

    The main.. means “the commits on this branch that aren’t on main”.

    OUTPUT 

    d8cc138 readme
9e1626f try smoothing
4244130 fix typo
2b17bef cli stuff
9a6471e remove print
89f7c6f add tests
33aa1de fix
21dd6b4 tidy up
ead2b48 wip
cd6792e add background module

    You wrote a list in episode 3 of the commits you wished the branch contained. Ours was:

    1. Handle constant spectra in normalise
    2. Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows
    3. Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks
    4. Add rolling minimum background subtraction
    5. Add tests for background subtraction
    6. Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
    7. Document --subtract-background in the README

    Compare it with yours. Today we turn the branch into that list. None of the code changes. We only change the story of how it got there.

    Callout

    The golden rule, for now

    Only rewrite history that nobody else has. This branch is only on your computer (and maybe your fork), so it’s safe. We’ll see what goes wrong when you rewrite shared history in episode 9.

    First, a safety net

    Before changing anything, put a label on where you are:

    BASH 

    git branch backup/background-subtraction

    It’s a second name for the current tip (remember, a branch is just a label), so whatever happens we can get back. You also have git rebase --abort, which stops a rebase and puts everything back, and the reflog from episode 4.

    What does rebase do?

    Rebase takes some commits and replays them one at a time on top of a starting point. Each replayed commit is a new commit, with a new hash (episode 2: a changed commit, or a changed parent, means a new hash). “Interactive” means git stops first and lets you say what to do with each commit.

    Before:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {The branch before the rebase}
    accDescr: {The branch background-subtraction has four commits, A, B, C and D, on top of main.}
    bs(["background-subtraction"]) --> D --> C --> B --> A --> main

    After git rebase -i main, dropping C and combining A and B:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {The branch after the rebase, with the old commits kept by the backup branch}
    accDescr: {The branch background-subtraction now has two new commits, A B prime and D prime, on top of main, shown in green. The old commits A, B, C and D still exist, shown dashed, and the backup branch points at them.}
    bs(["background-subtraction"]) --> Dp["D'"] --> ABp["AB'"] --> main
    bk(["backup/background-subtraction"]) --> D --> C --> B --> A --> main
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    classDef old stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class Dp,ABp new
    class D,C,B,A old

    Green: new commits made by the rebase. Dashed: the old commits, kept by the backup branch. Older commits are on the left.

    The todo list

    Start an interactive rebase onto main. That’s where our branch began, so every commit on the branch since then gets replayed:

    BASH 

    git rebase -i main

    Your editor opens with a list of every commit on the branch. It’s the opposite order from git log: the oldest is at the top, because that’s the order git will replay them in.

    pick cd6792e add background module
pick ead2b48 wip
pick 21dd6b4 tidy up
pick 33aa1de fix
pick 89f7c6f add tests
pick 9a6471e remove print
pick 2b17bef cli stuff
pick 4244130 fix typo
pick 9e1626f try smoothing
pick d8cc138 readme

# Rebase 1e81f27..d8cc138 onto 1e81f27 (10 commands)
# ...

    Git will do the lines from top to bottom, one at a time. You change what happens by changing the word at the start of a line, or by moving lines (in VS Code, Alt+↑ and Alt+↓ move the current line):

    Command What it does to the commit
    pick keep it as it is
    reword keep it, but let me change the message
    edit stop here so I can change the commit (or split it)
    squash merge it into the commit above it, and let me combine the messages
    fixup merge it into the commit above it, and throw away its message
    drop throw it away

    Deleting a line is the same as drop. For now, close the editor without changing anything: git replays all ten commits as they were, and nothing happens.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: which command?

    For each of these, which command from the table would you use?

    1. A commit message says oops, but the change itself is fine.
    2. A commit adds a file you were only experimenting with.
    3. Two commits are really one change that you made in two goes, and you only want to keep the first message.
    1. reword
    2. drop
    3. fixup (or squash if you want to write a new message combining both)

    Rebase 1: the easy fixes, all at once

    We’ll do this in two rebases. In the first we deal with everything that is dropping, rewording, moving or folding in. In the second, which is your challenge, we’ll split a commit.

    First, work out what each commit really is:

    Commit What it really is
    add background module the start of the feature: a new file with a first version of the function
    wip carries on writing that function
    tidy up three unrelated fixes, nothing to do with the feature (we’ll split it in the next rebase)
    fix fixes a bug in the function
    add tests tests for the function
    remove print removes a debugging print from the function
    cli stuff adds the --subtract-background option, but the message says nothing
    fix typo fixes a typo in the function’s docstring
    try smoothing an experiment that nothing uses
    readme documents the new option
    Challenge

    Challenge: choose the commands

    Now decide a command for each, using the table of commands above. Three things to think about:

    • Which commits are just corrections that belong inside another commit?
    • Which commit doesn’t belong with the feature at all, and should come first?
    • Which commit shouldn’t be here, and which has a message that tells you nothing?

    Then start the rebase, edit the list, and save:

    BASH 

    git rebase -i main

    Git will open the editor again for the reword, so you can type the new message. When it finishes, check your work:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..
git diff --stat backup/background-subtraction

    You should have five commits, and the only difference from the backup should be the file from the commit you dropped.

    The finished todo list:

    pick 21dd6b4 tidy up
pick cd6792e add background module
fixup ead2b48 wip
fixup 33aa1de fix
fixup 9a6471e remove print
fixup 4244130 fix typo
pick 89f7c6f add tests
reword 2b17bef cli stuff
pick d8cc138 readme
drop 9e1626f try smoothing

    Why:

    • tidy up moves to the top: the feature doesn’t depend on it, so it comes first. It’s still pick for now.
    • wip, fix, remove print and fix typo are all corrections to add background module, so they sit right under it, as fixup.
    • cli stuff is reword: change the message to Add --subtract-background option to the CLI.
    • try smoothing is drop.

    (We could move these commits because they changed different files from the ones they jumped over. If you try to move a commit above one that changed the same lines, git stops with a conflict. Resolve it, or git rebase --abort and rethink the order.)

    The result (your hashes will be different from ours):

    OUTPUT 

    d71e0a5 readme
bddb2b7 Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
4d0a337 add tests
2383a68 add background module
734a867 tidy up

    OUTPUT 

     scratch_smoothing.py | 5 -----
 1 file changed, 5 deletions(-)
    Callout

    squash or fixup?

    squash does the same as fixup, but opens an editor so you can write a message that combines both. Use fixup when the later commit is just a correction, and squash when both commits have something worth saying.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: where did the old commits go?

    Compare git log --oneline main.. with git log --oneline backup/background-subtraction.

    1. Why does every commit on your branch have a new hash, even tidy up, which you didn’t change?
    2. Where have the old ten commits gone? Did try smoothing vanish from the repository entirely?
    1. tidy up now sits on a different parent (it moved to the top, so its parent is now main), and rebase always makes a new commit when it replays one. A hash covers the contents and the parent, so the hash changes (episode 2).
    2. Nothing is gone. The old commits are still there, and backup/background-subtraction still points at them. try smoothing is only out of your branch. It’s in the reflog too (episode 4).

    Pause here until everyone has five commits. The commonest problems are:

    • The editor opened in vim (not VS Code), so core.editor wasn’t set. Fix it with git config --global core.editor "code --wait". If they are stuck in vim: :q! aborts the rebase step.
    • Typing in the wrong order. Remember it’s oldest first.
    • Saving the file but not closing the VS Code tab. Git waits until the tab is closed.
    • A commit moved above one that touches the same file, and a conflict. They can git rebase --abort and start again, with the todo list given in the solution.

    Rebase 2: split a commit

    Five commits now, and one of them is still doing too much: tidy up. Look at what is inside it (it’s the first commit on the branch):

    BASH 

    git show --stat HEAD~4

    OUTPUT 

    commit 734a867...
Author: Sam Scientist <sam.scientist@example.org>

    tidy up

 peakfinder/io.py        | 6 +++---
 peakfinder/normalise.py | 5 ++++-
 peakfinder/peaks.py     | 2 ++
 tests/test_normalise.py | 4 ++++
 tests/test_peaks.py     | 7 +++++++
 5 files changed, 20 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)

    It has three unrelated fixes. A reviewer has to work out which hunk belongs to which idea.

    Challenge

    Challenge: split a commit, and finish the messages

    Using an interactive rebase and the edit command, split tidy up into these three commits:

    1. Handle constant spectra in normalise (normalise.py and its test)
    2. Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows (io.py)
    3. Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks (peaks.py and its test)

    In the same rebase, give the other vague messages proper ones (hint: reword):

    • add background module becomes Add rolling minimum background subtraction
    • add tests becomes Add tests for background subtraction
    • readme becomes Document --subtract-background in the README

    Hints:

    • edit stops the rebase after applying the commit. You then need to undo the commit, but keep its changes in your working files. Which reset do you want? (Episode 5: mixed. In VS Code, Undo Last Commit, then Unstage All Changes.)
    • Stage each group of files in the Source Control view (or git add <files>), then commit.
    • When you have made your three commits, tell git to carry on.
    • git status tells you what to do next, at any time.

    When you finish, check your work:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..
git diff --stat backup/background-subtraction

    You should have seven commits, and a diff that only shows scratch_smoothing.py.

    Start the rebase. Change pick to edit for tidy up, and to reword for the three vague messages. (Use the hashes from your log.)

    BASH 

    git rebase -i main
    edit 734a867 tidy up
reword 2383a68 add background module
reword 4d0a337 add tests
pick bddb2b7 Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
reword d71e0a5 readme

    Git stops at tidy up. The commit has been applied, and HEAD is that commit. Undo the commit but keep the changes:

    BASH 

    git reset HEAD^
git status --short

    OUTPUT 

     M peakfinder/io.py
 M peakfinder/normalise.py
 M peakfinder/peaks.py
 M tests/test_normalise.py
 M tests/test_peaks.py

    Make three commits:

    BASH 

    git add peakfinder/normalise.py tests/test_normalise.py
git commit -m "Handle constant spectra in normalise"

git add peakfinder/io.py
git commit -m "Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows"

git add peakfinder/peaks.py tests/test_peaks.py
git commit -m "Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks"

    Carry on with the rebase. It will stop at each reword so you can type the new message.

    BASH 

    git rebase --continue

    Finally:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..

    OUTPUT 

    16dc9b1 Document --subtract-background in the README
5f580ee Add --subtract-background option to the CLI
0c4a936 Add tests for background subtraction
2917647 Add rolling minimum background subtraction
28ec0e5 Check x and y are the same length in find_peaks
5d3c64c Let load_spectrum skip a variable number of header rows
0e4303b Handle constant spectra in normalise

    (Your hashes will be different.)

    Give people about 10 to 12 minutes, then review it together. Live-demo the solution in the VS Code terminal while someone describes what they did.

    Make sure nobody merges background-subtraction into main at the end. Tomorrow, main has to be unchanged so that the colleague’s branch can be fast-forwarded onto it (episode 9). If anyone does, git reset --hard origin/main on main puts it right.

    Things that commonly go wrong:

    • Forgetting git rebase --continue after the split. git status says “interactive rebase in progress”.
    • git reset --hard instead of git reset. The changes are gone from the working directory! Show them how to recover: git rebase --abort, then start rebase 2 again.
    • Staged everything in one go, ending with a single commit again. Check with git show --stat.
    • A conflict in a reword step. This shouldn’t happen in this exercise. If it does, git rebase --abort and restart.
    • Someone who is hopelessly lost: have them git rebase --abort (if in a rebase), then git reset --hard backup/background-subtraction, and go again from rebase 1. If they have no backup, a helper can give them the clean result (see the instructor guide for the rescue commands).

    Look at the result

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..

    Compare this to the log at the start of the episode, and to the list you wrote in episode 3. The code didn’t change, but a reviewer can now:

    • read one commit at a time, each with a single purpose
    • trust the messages to say why the change was made
    • look at the three small fixes separately from the feature

    In real life, the next step would be to push this branch and open a pull request for review (we’ll do that in episode 11, with a different branch). Once approved, it would be merged into main.

    We aren’t going to merge this one. It was practice, and tomorrow’s story needs main to stay exactly as it is. So leave it where it is. It has done its job.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: when would you not do this?

    Think about these three situations. In which would you be happy to rewrite history, and in which not?

    1. A branch that only exists on your laptop.
    2. A branch you pushed to your fork, with an open pull request that someone has started reviewing.
    3. main in a repository the whole team uses.
    1. Happy. Nobody else is affected.
    2. Careful. Possible, and quite common, but the reviewer has to be told: we’ll see how to do it well in episode 11.
    3. Never. Everybody else’s copies have the old commits, and rewriting would put the team’s histories out of step.
    Key Points
    • git rebase -i <base> lets you edit every commit on a branch since <base>
    • The todo list is oldest first: change the command word to reword, drop, fixup or edit, and move lines to reorder
    • Rebase makes new commits. The old ones remain, so a backup branch or the reflog gets you back
    • Use edit and git reset HEAD^ to split a commit into several
    • git rebase --abort undoes a rebase that is going badly
    • Only rewrite history that nobody else has yet

    Content from The Daily Loop: Fixup and Autosquash

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 36 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I keep my history clean while I’m still working?
    • How do I fix a mistake in an earlier commit without a “fix typo” commit?

    Objectives

    • Plan a few commits, then build a feature one atomic commit at a time
    • Use git commit --fixup to correct an earlier commit
    • Use git rebase -i --autosquash to fold the fixups in
    • Push a tidy branch to your fork

    The loop

    In the last episode we rescued a messy branch. That was useful, but nobody wants to do it every time. Here is the habit that means you rarely need to:

    flowchart TD
    accTitle: {The daily loop}
    accDescr: {A flowchart. Plan the commits, then make a small change and commit it. If you spot a mistake in an earlier commit, make a fixup commit for it. Repeat while there is more to do. When the work is done, run an interactive rebase with autosquash, then push and ask for review.}
    P["Plan the commits"] --> C["Make a small change<br/>and commit it"]
    C --> Q{"Spot a mistake in<br/>an EARLIER commit?"}
    Q -->|yes| F["git commit<br/>--fixup (that commit)"]
    Q -->|no| M{"More to do?"}
    F --> M
    M -->|yes| C
    M -->|no| A["Tidy up before sharing:<br/>git rebase -i<br/>--autosquash main<br/>(fixups, then reword,<br/>reorder or drop as needed)"]
    A --> S["Push, and ask for review"]

    The idea: commit freely as you go, and tidy up before you share. You never have to stop and interrupt your flow to edit history. You leave a note (“this is a fix for that commit”) and tidy up at the end.

    Start from a fresh branch

    Always start new work from an up-to-date main, on a branch of its own:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git status                      # should say "nothing to commit, working tree clean"
git switch -c min-height

    (git switch -c creates the branch and moves you onto it. In real life you’d git pull first, and your pull.rebase true setting means that keeps history linear too.)

    Plan

    Remember episode 3? First, the overall change, in one sentence: “Ignore peaks that are lower than a minimum height, because our example data reports far too many.” Then the steps along the way, which is our commit plan:

    1. Add a min_height option to find_peaks
2. Add tests for min_height

    Why bother? Look at what the program does on our example data right now:

    BASH 

    python -m peakfinder.cli data/example_spectrum.csv | wc -l

    OUTPUT 

    71

    71 “peaks”, but there are only three real ones. The rest are noise. A minimum height will help.

    Build it

    Commit 1. In peakfinder/peaks.py, add the option and use it. Only these lines change:

    PYTHON 

    def find_peaks(x, y, min_height=None):
    ...
        if y[i] > y[i - 1] and y[i] > y[i + 1]:
            if min_height is None or y[i] >= min_height:
                peaks.append((x[i], y[i]))

    BASH 

    git commit -am "Add min_height option to find_peaks"

    Commit 2. Add a test at the end of tests/test_peaks.py:

    PYTHON 

    

def test_min_height_ignores_small_peaks():
    x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
    y = [0, 3, 0, 1, 4, 1, 0]
    assert find_peaks(x, y, min_height=3.5) == [(4, 4)]

    BASH 

    pytest
git commit -am "Add tests for min_height"

    Read your own work, and leave a note

    Before you share a branch, review it yourself, the way a reviewer will. In VS Code, open the Source Control view and look at the Graph section (below the lists of changes). It shows the commits on your branch. Click one to see which files it touched, and click a file to see that commit’s changes by themselves. (On the command line: git log --oneline main.. and git show <hash>.)

    Looking at commit 1, you notice something: the function’s docstring doesn’t mention the new option. That’s a correction to commit 1, not a new idea, and it shouldn’t be a commit of its own on the end. Edit the docstring in peaks.py:

    PYTHON 

        """Return a list of (position, height) for each local maximum in y.

    Peaks lower than min_height are ignored, if it is given.
    """

    git commit --fixup <commit> makes a new commit whose message is fixup! followed by the subject of the commit it corrects. It’s a note to your future self: “this belongs inside that commit”. Find the hash, stage the change (+ next to the file in the Source Control view), and commit it as a fixup of commit 1:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..
git commit --fixup <hash of "Add min_height option to find_peaks">
git log --oneline main..

    OUTPUT 

    cfcb779 fixup! Add min_height option to find_peaks
3eace0b Add tests for min_height
d1bc7ff Add min_height option to find_peaks

    VS Code has no button for --fixup, so this is one of the few places we use the terminal. The pattern that works well: stage in the Source Control view, commit in the terminal.

    Tidy up before sharing: autosquash

    When you’re ready to share, you do one last interactive rebase. It has two jobs:

    1. Fold in the fixups, which --autosquash does for you.
    2. Tidy anything else, using the same todo list as episode 6: reword a message that’s gone stale, drop a commit that turned out to be unnecessary, edit one that should be split, or move lines to reorder. Keep going until the list of commits reads well.

    BASH 

    git rebase -i --autosquash main

    Here is what happens to the branch:

    Before:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {The branch before autosquash}
    accDescr: {Three commits on top of main. From the oldest: Add min_height option, then Add tests for min_height, then a fixup commit on the end, shown in yellow, which corrects the first commit.}
    branch(["min-height"]) --> F["fixup! Add min_height option"] --> T["Add tests for min_height"] --> O["Add min_height option"] --> main
    classDef fix fill:#ffd,stroke:#a80,color:#000
    class F fix

    After:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {The branch after autosquash}
    accDescr: {Two commits on top of main, shown in green because they are new. The fixup has been folded into the first commit, so Add min_height option now includes the docstring change, and Add tests for min_height follows it.}
    branch(["min-height"]) --> T["Add tests for min_height"] --> O["Add min_height option<br/>(now with the docstring)"] --> main
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class T,O new

    Yellow: a fixup note. Green: new commits made by the rebase. Older commits are on the left.

    Your editor opens, and git has already moved the fixup under the commit it belongs to, and marked it fixup:

    pick d1bc7ff Add min_height option to find_peaks
fixup cfcb779 fixup! Add min_height option to find_peaks
pick 3eace0b Add tests for min_height

    This time there is nothing else to edit, so just save and close. (If your commit list needs more, this is the moment: change the words in the todo list before you save, exactly as in episode 6.)

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..

    OUTPUT 

    37552d4 Add tests for min_height
43922bf Add min_height option to find_peaks

    Two clean commits, in the order you planned them, and the missing docstring never appears in the history as a “fix” commit.

    Callout

    --autosquash and rebase.autoSquash

    In the setup page you set rebase.autoSquash true, which makes git rebase -i do this automatically. Typing --autosquash as well does no harm, and works on a computer where the setting isn’t there.

    Callout

    Does every commit still pass?

    Remember “atomic” means each commit works on its own. You can ask git to check, by running the tests after every commit of the rebase:

    BASH 

    git rebase main --exec "pytest -q"

    It stops at the first commit where the tests fail. This is a great final check before asking for a review.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: which commit?

    For each, which commit should the fix be a --fixup of?

    1. Your three commits are add a function, add the option that uses it, add tests. The test shows a bug in the function.
    2. You spot a typo in a comment you added two commits ago.
    3. You forgot to update the README, which is a new thing and goes with none of your commits.
    1. The commit that added the function. That’s where the bug was born.
    2. The commit that added the comment.
    3. None of them. If it’s a new, separate change, make an ordinary new commit (such as Document the new option in the README). --fixup is for corrections to earlier commits.

    Push your branch

    Your branch is tidy. Push it to your fork:

    BASH 

    git push

    Because of your push.autoSetupRemote setting, git creates the branch on GitHub and links it up for you. We aren’t opening a pull request yet. That’s on day 2.
