    Challenge

    Challenge: your own feature

    You’ve seen the loop with min_height. Now do it again, for a different feature. You and your partner each take one:

    • Feature A: min_prominence. Only keep peaks that stand out from their surroundings. (Whoever’s first name comes first alphabetically.)
    • Feature B: peak widths. Optionally return each peak’s width at half its height. (The other person.)

    The code is provided below. Your job is the workflow, not the maths.

    Start from main, on your own branch:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git switch -c feature-prominence      # or feature-widths

    Your plan (write it down before you start!):

    1. Add a helper function to peaks.py
2. Add an option to find_peaks that uses it
3. Add a test

    Follow it, committing after each step, with a good message for each. Then, when the test fails, fix the problem in the right commit using --fixup and --autosquash.

    Finally, check each commit passes, and push the branch.

    Feature A: prominence

    Commit 1. Add this to the end of peakfinder/peaks.py. Commit message: Add prominence function

    PYTHON 

    

def prominence(y, i):
    """Height of the peak at i above the higher of the valleys either side."""
    left_min = y[i]
    for j in range(i - 1, -1, -1):
        if y[j] > y[i]:
            break
        left_min = min(left_min, y[j])
    right_min = y[i]
    for j in range(i + 1, len(y)):
        if y[j] > y[i]:
            break
        right_min = min(right_min, y[j])
    return y[i] - min(left_min, right_min)

    Commit 2. Change find_peaks in the same file. The signature gets a new option, and the append is wrapped in a check:

    PYTHON 

    def find_peaks(x, y, min_prominence=0):
    ...
        if y[i] > y[i - 1] and y[i] > y[i + 1]:
            if prominence(y, i) >= min_prominence:
                peaks.append((x[i], y[i]))

    Commit message: Add min_prominence option to find_peaks

    Commit 3. Add this test to the end of tests/test_peaks.py. Commit message: Add tests for min_prominence

    PYTHON 

    

def test_min_prominence_ignores_bumps_on_a_slope():
    x = list(range(8))
    y = [0, 5, 4, 4.5, 4, 3, 1, 0]
    assert find_peaks(x, y, min_prominence=1) == [(1, 5)]

    Feature B: widths

    Commit 1. Add this to the end of peakfinder/peaks.py. Commit message: Add peak_width function

    PYTHON 

    

def peak_width(x, y, i):
    """Width of the peak at i where it falls to half its height."""
    half = y[i] / 2
    left = i
    while left > 0 and y[left] >= half:
        left -= 1
    right = i
    while right < len(y) - 1 and y[right] >= half:
        right += 1
    return x[right] - x[left]

    Commit 2. Change find_peaks in the same file. The signature gets a new option, and the append changes:

    PYTHON 

    def find_peaks(x, y, with_widths=False):
    ...
        if y[i] > y[i - 1] and y[i] > y[i + 1]:
            if with_widths:
                peaks.append((x[i], y[i], peak_width(x, y, i)))
            else:
                peaks.append((x[i], y[i]))

    Commit message: Add with_widths option to find_peaks

    Commit 3. Add this test to the end of tests/test_peaks.py. Commit message: Add tests for peak widths

    PYTHON 

    

def test_peak_widths():
    x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
    y = [0, 1, 4, 8, 4, 1, 0]
    assert find_peaks(x, y, with_widths=True) == [(3, 8, 2)]

    Then, for both

    1. Run pytest before you commit the test. It fails. Read the failure, and think about which commit the bug came from.
    2. Fix the bug. (Hint for A: the docstring says the higher of the two valleys. Hint for B: should the half-height point itself count as inside the peak?)
    3. Make the fix a --fixup of the commit that introduced the bug, and commit the test as a normal commit.
    4. Run git rebase -i --autosquash main, and just save the todo list.
    5. Check: git log --oneline main.. shows three clean commits, with no fixup!. Then git rebase main --exec "pytest -q" passes.
    6. git push

    The bug. In A, the function used min(left_min, right_min) and should use max(...). In B, both while loops used >= and should use >.

    The workflow (A shown; B is the same with different names):

    BASH 

    git switch main
git switch -c feature-prominence

# commit 1: paste the helper at the end of peaks.py
git commit -am "Add prominence function"

# commit 2: edit find_peaks
git commit -am "Add min_prominence option to find_peaks"

# write the test (don't commit yet)
pytest                          # fails!
# fix min -> max in prominence()
git log --oneline main..        # find the hash of "Add prominence function"
git add peakfinder/peaks.py
git commit --fixup <hash>       # the hash of commit 1
git add tests/test_peaks.py
git commit -m "Add tests for min_prominence"

git rebase -i --autosquash main # save and close the todo list
git log --oneline main..
git rebase main --exec "pytest -q"
git push

    The log before autosquash:

    OUTPUT 

    bb3dfef Add tests for min_prominence
59ccff4 fixup! Add prominence function
9a044d1 Add min_prominence option to find_peaks
29261e9 Add prominence function

    and after:

    OUTPUT 

    e6a6edb Add tests for min_prominence
20567d6 Add min_prominence option to find_peaks
535b14d Add prominence function

    Notice the fixup crossed over commit 2 to land in commit 1, which is where the bug was.

    Demo (about 8 minutes, with learners following). It’s deliberately short: two commits, one docstring fixup, and the autosquash. People copy the code from the page, so the demo is about the git. The key moments to slow down for:

    1. Spotting the missing docstring, and the thought “this belongs to commit 1, not a new commit.” Say it out loud.
    2. The fixup! commit at the end of the log, then the todo list with the fixup line already moved up under its commit. Pause here. People find this a pleasant surprise.
    3. The log afterwards: no fixup, nothing to hide.

    Save the time for the challenge, where they do it all themselves (and meet a bug that a test catches).

    Challenge (28 minutes). Pairs: each person works alone on their own computer, but can ask the other. Online: breakout rooms of two.

    Common problems:

    • git commit --fixup with a wrong hash (or a hash from before an earlier rebase). git log --oneline main.. and try again. If the fixup is wrong, git reset --soft HEAD^ and redo it.
    • The test doesn’t fail. They fixed the bug while writing the helper. Tell them to paste the code exactly as written.
    • B: only one >= fixed. The test still fails. Both loops need changing.
    • Autosquash doesn’t reorder anything. They ran git rebase main without -i (no autosquash), or the rebase.autoSquash setting is missing. Use git rebase -i --autosquash main.
    • Editor doesn’t open or hangs. core.editor isn’t code --wait (see setup).
    • A conflict during autosquash. Rare here. git rebase --abort, and check the fixup only touches the lines it should.

    Pushing: git push needs authentication to work, which was part of the setup. If someone’s push fails, pair them with a helper rather than losing time. They can still finish the exercise locally, and push later.

    End of day 1. Before finishing, check everyone has:

    • a pushed branch (feature-prominence or feature-widths) on their fork
    • main unchanged, and a clean git status

    Preview day 2: “Overnight, a colleague’s pull request gets merged into main. It touches the same function as yours…”

    Key Points
    • Plan a few commits, then commit small changes as you go
    • When you spot a mistake in an earlier commit, git commit --fixup <commit> leaves a note, without stopping your flow
    • Before sharing, git rebase -i --autosquash main folds each fixup into its target, and you can also reword, reorder, drop or edit commits until the history reads well
    • git rebase main --exec "pytest -q" checks every commit passes

    Content from Day 2 Recap and Warm-up

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 9 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What did we cover yesterday?
    • Is everyone ready to start?

    Objectives

    • Recall the main ideas from day 1
    • Check your branch and your fork are as we left them

    Yesterday in one minute

    Yesterday we were the author. We learned:

    • A commit is a snapshot with a pointer to its parent, and a branch is just a label. Changing a commit makes a new one.
    • The reflog remembers where HEAD has been, so we can recover from mistakes.
    • Good commits are atomic: one logical change, with the project working at every step.
    • We can shape commits with the staging area, --amend and reset, and rewrite a branch with interactive rebase.
    • In our daily loop we commit as we go, leave --fixup notes for mistakes in earlier commits, and tidy up with git rebase -i --autosquash before sharing.

    Today we’re a collaborator. Other people’s work is landing in the same project as ours, and we need to work with it.

    Warm-up quiz

    Try these on your own for a minute or two, then we’ll go through them together.

    Challenge

    Quiz

    1. When you make a new commit, what happens to the branch label?
    2. Why does git commit --amend give you a different hash?
    3. You made a fixup! commit for something three commits back. How do you fold it into the right commit?
    4. You lost a commit after a mistake. Where do you look to find it?
    5. Why do we try to make each commit atomic? Give one reason.
    1. It moves forward to the new commit. A branch is just a label that follows the newest commit.
    2. A commit’s hash is calculated from its contents, including the message and its parent. Change any of that and you get a new commit with a new hash.
    3. git rebase -i --autosquash main (or just git rebase -i main if rebase.autoSquash is on). It moves the fixup under its target and folds it in.
    4. The reflog: git reflog. Find the hash, then git reset --hard <hash> or git branch <name> <hash>.
    5. Any of: it’s easier to review one idea at a time; you can revert just the bad change; you can cherry-pick just the fix; git bisect finds a small, specific commit; each commit passes the tests.

    Check your state

    Make sure you’re ready for today. In your peakfinder clone, with your virtual environment active:

    BASH 

    git status
git switch main
git log --oneline -1
git branch
git log --oneline main..feature-prominence      # or feature-widths

    You should see:

    • git status: nothing to commit, working tree clean
    • main still at Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks (hash 1e81f27). If main has any extra commits of your own, you can put it right with git reset --hard origin/main.
    • Your feature branch listed, with three clean commits and no fixup!.

    Then check your work is on GitHub. Open your fork in the browser, switch to your feature branch, and check that you can see the three commits. Ask your partner to look too.

    Callout

    If you’re missing your feature branch

    If your branch is missing, or in a bad state, don’t spend long on it. Ask a helper, or build a quick replacement:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git switch -c feature-prominence

    and redo the three commits from episode 7 (it’s fast now that you’ve done it before). The helpers can also give you a ready-made branch.

    Today’s story

    While you were working on your feature, a colleague was working on the same project, and their work has now been approved and merged into main.

    Today we’ll:

    1. bring that work into our branch, and deal with the conflict between their changes and ours (episode 9)
    2. find out why a test is now failing, and which change caused it (episode 10)
    3. have our work reviewed by our partner (episode 11)
    4. set up automatic checks (episode 12)
    5. release a fix (episode 13)

    Two rules for today

    • Every pull request is on your own fork, never on the course repository. GitHub proposes the original repository by default, so we’ll remind you where it matters.
    • Merge pull requests with “Rebase and merge”, so your carefully made commits stay exactly as you wrote them.

    Keep this to about 10 minutes. The quiz can be done by a show of hands, or by cold-calling. Don’t let it turn into a lecture.

    State check. The point is to find the people with a broken day-1 state before they hit episode 9. Common problems:

    • main has local commits, because they committed to it by mistake. git reset --hard origin/main fixes it.
    • The feature branch still contains fixup! commits, so they never ran the autosquash. They can do it now: git rebase -i --autosquash main.
    • They never pushed. git push.
    • The fork is missing the colleague’s branch (they forked with the default-branch-only option). Tomorrow’s story needs colleague/normalise-modes. They can fetch it from the original repository (git remote add upstream <url>, git fetch upstream) and push it to their fork, but it’s often quicker to re-fork.

    Fallback branches. Have a ready-made feature-prominence and feature-widths available for anyone who lost theirs. These aren’t published to the learners’ forks, so give the helpers a way to hand them out.

    Key Points
    • Day 1 was about producing good history: snapshots, atomic commits, rewriting and the daily loop
    • Day 2 is about sharing it and working alongside other people’s changes
    • Check your branch and your fork are in order before starting

    Content from Rebase vs Merge, and Resolving Conflicts

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • My teammate’s work landed while I was working. How do I bring it into my branch?
    • What is the difference between merging and rebasing?
    • How do I resolve a conflict?
    • Why can’t I push after a rebase?

    Objectives

    • Explain the difference between merge and rebase using diagrams
    • Fast-forward main and see why it stays a straight line
    • Bring changes from main into a feature branch by rebasing
    • Resolve a conflict using the VS Code merge editor
    • Push a rebased branch safely with --force-with-lease
    • State the golden rule: don’t rewrite history other people are using

    While you were working

    Yesterday you built a feature on its own branch. Meanwhile, a colleague was working on the same project. Their pull request has just been approved, and merged into main. Our feature branch is now based on an out-of-date main:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Main has moved on while your branch stood still}
    accDescr: {A shared starting commit. Main now has the colleague's work on top of it. Your feature branch also starts from the same shared commit, but has your three commits and does not have the colleague's work.}
    main(["main"]) --> W["colleague's work<br/>(6 commits)"] --> base["starting point"]
    feature(["your feature"]) --> F3 --> F2 --> F1 --> base

    We need their changes in our branch, so that we can be sure our work fits with theirs before anyone reviews it.

    First, let’s simulate their pull request being merged. In real life GitHub does this when someone clicks the merge button. Your fork has a branch colleague/normalise-modes that stands in for their work:

    BASH 

    git fetch
git switch main
git merge --ff-only origin/colleague/normalise-modes
git push
git log --oneline --graph -8

    OUTPUT 

    * 1c13652 Document Peak in the README
* b83c177 Return Peak tuples from find_peaks
* df97539 Bump version to 0.2.0
* 25dbef6 Remove unused import from cli
* e2c7538 Add mode option to normalise
* 0b83055 Fix typo in README
* 1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks
* b7cf029 Add command line interface

    This was a fast-forward: main had nothing of its own, so git simply moved the main label along to the colleague’s last commit. No new commit was made, and the history is still a straight line. (--ff-only means “do this, or refuse”: it will never silently create a merge commit.)

    Before:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {Before the fast-forward}
    accDescr: {Main points at the starting point. The colleague's branch points at the colleague's six commits, which sit on top of the same starting point.}
    main(["main"]) --> base["starting point"]
    colleague(["colleague/normalise-modes"]) --> W["colleague's work<br/>(6 commits)"] --> base

    After:

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After the fast-forward}
    accDescr: {The main label has moved forward along the line to the colleague's last commit, so main and the colleague's branch point at the same commit. No new commit was made.}
    main(["main"]) --> W["colleague's work<br/>(6 commits)"]
    colleague(["colleague/normalise-modes"]) --> W
    W --> base["starting point"]

    Only the main label moved. Older commits are on the left.

    Two ways to bring it in

    There are two ways to get main’s new commits into your branch.

    Option 1: merge

    BASH 

    git merge main

    Git creates a merge commit that has two parents: the tip of your branch and the tip of main.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After merging main into your branch}
    accDescr: {A new merge commit sits on top of your branch. It has two parents: your last commit, and the colleague's work on main. The history is no longer a straight line, because it splits and joins.}
    main(["main"]) --> W["colleague's work"] --> base["starting point"]
    feature(["your feature"]) --> M["merge commit"]
    M --> F3 --> F2 --> F1 --> base
    M --> W
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class M new

    Green: the new merge commit. Everything else was there before the merge and hasn’t changed. Older commits are on the left.

    Nothing has been rewritten, and that is the merge’s great strength: it’s safe. But your history now splits and rejoins. Do that every time main moves, and your branch fills up with “Merge branch ‘main’ into …” commits that say nothing about your work. A reviewer reading commit by commit has to read around them.

    Callout

    Merge commits are git’s default, and a fine default

    Merging is what git does unless you tell it otherwise, and it’s the default button on GitHub (Create a merge commit). For most teams it’s a perfectly good default: it’s safe, it never rewrites anything, and it records exactly when branches were joined. We prefer a straight line because we want every commit to be readable one at a time, but a history with merge commits isn’t wrong. Follow your team’s convention.

    Option 2: rebase

    BASH 

    git rebase main

    Git takes your commits one at a time and replays them on top of the new main. This is the same thing as in episode 6, but the new starting point is different.

    flowchart RL
    accTitle: {After rebasing your branch onto main}
    accDescr: {Your three commits have been replayed on top of the colleague's work, so they are new commits, shown in green, with new hashes. The history is a straight line. The old versions of your commits still exist, shown dashed, but nothing points at them.}
    main(["main"]) --> W["colleague's work"] --> base["starting point"]
    feature(["your feature"]) --> F3p["F3'"] --> F2p["F2'"] --> F1p["F1'"] --> W
    F3 --> F2 --> F1 --> base
    classDef new fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    classDef old stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class F3p,F2p,F1p new
    class F3,F2,F1 old

    Green: new commits made by the rebase. Dashed: your old commits, which nothing points at now. Older commits are on the left.

    It is as if you had started your work after the colleague’s. History is a straight line, with your commits neatly on top.

    The difference in one sentence

    Merge joins the two tips together, and leaves a join in the history. Rebase moves the base (the bottom) of your branch to the tip of main, and leaves no trace of the move.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: merge or rebase?

    Which one:

    1. creates a new commit with two parents?
    2. gives every one of your commits a new hash?
    3. leaves a history that is a straight line?
    4. doesn’t change any existing commit?
    1. Merge
    2. Rebase (they are replayed on a new parent, so remember episode 2: new parent, new hash)
    3. Rebase
    4. Merge

    Watch: what a merge does

    Your instructor will demonstrate this on screen. Watch, and follow the output below, but don’t run these commands yourself. In a few minutes you’ll resolve this same conflict for real, in a rebase, and there’s no point doing it twice.

    The instructor switches to a feature branch and merges main into it:

    BASH 

    git switch feature-prominence
git merge main

    OUTPUT 

    Auto-merging tests/test_peaks.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in peakfinder/peaks.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

    A conflict. Git tried to combine the colleague’s changes with ours, but both of us changed the same lines of find_peaks, and git can’t decide whose change should win. It has stopped, and is waiting for us to decide.

    What is a conflict?

    Git merges changes automatically whenever it can. A conflict happens only when two sets of changes touch the same lines. Git marks the file with both versions. Open peakfinder/peaks.py and you’ll see something like:

    <<<<<<< HEAD
@dataclass
class Peak: ...
def find_peaks(x, y):
    """Return a list of Peak tuples, one for each local maximum in y."""
=======
def find_peaks(x, y, min_prominence=0):
    """Return a list of (position, height) for each local maximum in y."""
>>>>>>> your branch

    Everything between <<<<<<< and ======= is one side, and everything between ======= and >>>>>>> is the other. To resolve a conflict you edit the file so that it contains what you actually want, and delete the markers.

    You can do that by hand in any editor. VS Code has a much friendlier way.

    Resolving a conflict in VS Code

    1. Open the Source Control view. The conflicted file appears under Merge Changes.
    2. Click the file, and then Resolve in Merge Editor.
    3. The merge editor shows three panes:
      • Incoming (top left) and Current (top right): the two versions in conflict
      • Result (bottom): what the file will contain
    4. For each conflict, use the controls next to it to accept Incoming, accept Current, or accept both, or edit the Result directly. Most of the time you want a mix of both sides, so edit the result until it’s right. Check the Result after each choice: it tells you how many conflicts are still unresolved.
    5. When there are none left, click Complete Merge. VS Code saves the file and stages it. (It doesn’t finish the whole operation. See below.)

    (You can also resolve small conflicts without the merge editor, using the Accept Current Change / Accept Incoming Change / Accept Both Changes links that VS Code shows above each conflict in the file itself.)

    Callout

    “Current” and “Incoming” swap during a rebase

    In a merge, Current is your branch and Incoming is the branch you are merging in. That makes sense.

    In a rebase, it’s the other way round: Current is the branch you’re rebasing onto (here, main, with the colleague’s work), and Incoming is your commit being replayed. It’s confusing, but there’s a reason: git is building your commits on top of main, so main’s version is what’s already there.

    So always read the code, not the labels. Which side has the colleague’s changes, and which has yours?

    What do we want here?

    Both sides made a good change. The colleague wants find_peaks to return Peak objects, and you want to add your own option. We want both:

    • the colleague’s Peak class and the new docstring
    • your new parameter and your new filter, but building a Peak as the colleague did

    In the demonstration, the instructor resolves the conflict in the merge editor, then commits the merge:

    BASH 

    git commit --no-edit
git log --oneline --graph -8

    OUTPUT 

    *   01eb097 Merge branch 'main' into feature-prominence
|\
| * 1c13652 Document Peak in the README
| * b83c177 Return Peak tuples from find_peaks
| * df97539 Bump version to 0.2.0
| * 25dbef6 Remove unused import from cli
| * e2c7538 Add mode option to normalise
| * 0b83055 Fix typo in README
* | a340483 Test min_prominence

    There is the split and rejoin. We would rather not leave that in our history, so the instructor undoes the merge.

    Undoing the merge

    Before a merge, git remembered where it was in ORIG_HEAD (episode 4). That puts the branch back:

    BASH 

    git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
git log --oneline -4

    OUTPUT 

    a340483 Test min_prominence
c8e1c74 Add min_prominence option to find_peaks
7c8cefd Add prominence function
1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks

    The three commits are back, exactly as they were. (If this ever doesn’t work, the reflog has the answer.)

    Challenge

    Challenge: rebase onto main

    Now it’s your turn, the other way round. You’ve seen how a conflict gets resolved, so this time you do it, in a rebase. Switch to your feature branch, rebase it onto main, and resolve the conflict in the merge editor.

    BASH 

    git switch feature-prominence        # or feature-widths
git rebase main

    Git replays your three commits. It stops at the one that conflicts (your “Add … option to find_peaks” commit). Then:

    1. Open the Source Control view and resolve peaks.py in the merge editor. The result must have the colleague’s Peak tuple and your new option. There are two conflicts in the file, near the top and in the if inside the loop. (Hints are below.)
    2. Click Complete Merge. That stages the file.
    3. Tell git to carry on: git rebase --continue in the terminal. (VS Code’s Commit button also continues an in-progress rebase once everything is staged. An editor tab may open with the commit message. Just close it.)
    4. Run git log --oneline --graph -8: it should be a straight line, with your three commits on top of the colleague’s.
    5. Run the tests: pytest.

    Predict first: what do you expect pytest to say? Then look.

    Hints, for what the finished find_peaks needs:

    • Feature A (prominence): keep the colleague’s Peak class and docstring, add your min_prominence=0 parameter, and in the loop keep your if prominence(...) check, but append Peak(x[i], y[i]).
    • Feature B (widths): keep the colleague’s Peak class and docstring, add your with_widths=False parameter, and in the loop keep your if with_widths: branch. In the else branch append Peak(x[i], y[i]).

    If it all goes wrong, git rebase --abort puts everything back as it was before you started. (In VS Code: Command Palette, Git: Abort Rebase.)

    Feature A (the top of peaks.py, and the loop):

    PYTHON 

    from typing import NamedTuple

import numpy as np


class Peak(NamedTuple):
    position: float
    height: float


def find_peaks(x, y, min_prominence=0):
    """Return a list of Peak tuples, one for each local maximum in y."""
    x = np.asarray(x)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    peaks = []
    for i in range(1, len(y) - 1):
        if y[i] > y[i - 1] and y[i] > y[i + 1]:
            if prominence(y, i) >= min_prominence:
                peaks.append(Peak(x[i], y[i]))
    return peaks

    Feature B:

    PYTHON 

    def find_peaks(x, y, with_widths=False):
    """Return a list of Peak tuples, one for each local maximum in y."""
    x = np.asarray(x)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    peaks = []
    for i in range(1, len(y) - 1):
        if y[i] > y[i - 1] and y[i] > y[i + 1]:
            if with_widths:
                peaks.append((x[i], y[i], peak_width(x, y, i)))
            else:
                peaks.append(Peak(x[i], y[i]))
    return peaks

    (with the same Peak class above it.)

    The commands:

    BASH 

    git rebase main
# resolve peaks.py in the merge editor, then Complete Merge
git rebase --continue
git log --oneline --graph -8
pytest

    OUTPUT 

    * 8c01021 Test min_prominence
* 706f2cd Add min_prominence option to find_peaks
* cdd94be Add prominence function
* 1c13652 Document Peak in the README
* b83c177 Return Peak tuples from find_peaks
* df97539 Bump version to 0.2.0
* 25dbef6 Remove unused import from cli
* e2c7538 Add mode option to normalise
* 0b83055 Fix typo in README
* 1e81f27 Add plotting of the spectrum and its peaks

    A straight line: the colleague’s six commits, then your three.

    What does pytest say? All your tests pass, but there is one failure:

    OUTPUT 

    FAILED tests/test_normalise.py::test_normalise_runs_from_zero_to_one - assert...
1 failed, 8 passed

    That’s not in your code. It’s in normalise, which you haven’t touched. Something has changed in the colleague’s commits that affects it, and we’ll find out what in the next episode.

    Why can’t I push?

    Your branch is on GitHub from yesterday, with the old versions of your commits. Try to push the new ones:

    BASH 

    git push

    OUTPUT 

     ! [rejected]        feature-prominence -> feature-prominence (non-fast-forward)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind
hint: its remote counterpart. If you want to integrate the remote changes,
hint: use 'git pull' before pushing again.

    Git refuses, because the history on GitHub and the history on your computer have diverged. The remote has your three old commits, and you have three new ones that are replacements. It’s the picture from episode 2: a rebase makes new commits, and the old ones are still out there.

    Callout

    Don’t follow the hint!

    Git suggests git pull. Don’t. That would try to combine your new commits with the old ones on the remote. You’d end up with each commit twice, or a mess of conflicts.

    (We tried it. With git’s default, each of your commits ends up in the history twice, and you get a conflict. With pull.rebase true, git tries to replay the colleague’s commits on top of the old versions of yours and stops with conflicts. If you ever do it by accident, git merge --abort or git rebase --abort puts you back, and git reflog can help, as in episode 4.)

    What we want is to replace the remote’s version with ours. That is a force push, and it’s the correct thing to do after a rebase, as long as the only person whose work you’re replacing is you. Use the safe version:

    BASH 

    git push --force-with-lease

    OUTPUT 

     + a340483...36fc668 feature-prominence -> feature-prominence (forced update)

    The difference from --force:

    • --force says: “Overwrite the remote, whatever is there.”
    • --force-with-lease says: “Overwrite the remote, but only if it’s still what I last saw.”

    If a teammate had pushed something to the branch since you last fetched, --force-with-lease would refuse, instead of silently destroying their work. So always use it, and never plain --force.

    Callout

    The golden rule

    Only rewrite history that nobody else is depending on.

    • Your own feature branch, before anyone has built on it: fine.
    • A branch with an open pull request: fine, with care. The reviewer must know. We’ll cover that in episode 11.
    • main, or any branch other people have pulled and are working on: never.

    A word on linear history

    Our main is a straight line, and so is our branch. Many teams like this because:

    • git log reads like a story
    • bisect, blame and cherry-pick are easier
    • a revert undoes one thing

    When you merge a pull request on GitHub, there are three buttons. (The first, Create a merge commit, is the default, and a fine choice if that’s what your team does.)

    Button What it does to main Keeps your carefully made commits?
    Create a merge commit adds a merge commit with two parents yes, with a join in the history
    Squash and merge squashes all your commits into one no, it throws the story away
    Rebase and merge replays your commits on top of main yes, and the history stays straight

    If you took the trouble to curate your commits, rebase and merge is usually what you want. Squash is a reasonable fallback for a branch that nobody tidied up. Each team has its own policy, and it’s worth finding out what yours is.

    Callout

    Your pull.rebase setting

    You ran git config --global pull.rebase true in the setup. It makes a plain git pull rebase your local commits on top, instead of creating a merge commit. That’s a matter of taste (git’s default is to merge), but it keeps your branch a straight line.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check: is it safe to rebase?

    Which of these are OK to rebase and force-push (with --force-with-lease)?

    1. main
    2. A branch where you and your partner both push commits
    3. Your own feature branch with an open pull request that nobody has reviewed yet
    1. No. Everyone’s work is based on it.
    2. Only if you tell your partner, and they know to fetch and reset, or rebase. Otherwise they’ll have the old commits and be confused. Better to agree a rule first.
    3. Yes. It’s your branch. If no one has started reviewing, there’s nothing to disturb. (If they have, tell them. See episode 11.)

    Plan (about 35 minutes). Roughly: 10 minutes of explanation with the diagrams, 5 to fast-forward main, 5 for your demonstration of the merge (conflict, merge editor, graph, undo), 8 for the rebase challenge on their own, and 5 for the push and the buttons. The merge is a demo: learners watch and don’t type, so they resolve the conflict once, themselves, in the rebase. If you’re running short, skip the demo: the diagram already shows the double back.

    The demo is where you teach the merge editor. Open it, explain the three panes, and say out loud “which side has the colleague’s change, and which has mine?” before clicking anything. Then they do the same, alone, in the rebase.

    Roles swap in a rebase. Current and Incoming mean the opposite of merge. This catches everyone out. Spend a minute on the callout.

    Common problems:

    • They click “Accept Current” or “Accept Incoming” on a whole conflict and lose half of what they wanted. Check that the result has both Peak(...) and their new option (git diff main should show their feature). pytest will also fail with a NameError or TypeError.
    • They leave the markers in (<<<<<<<). git diff --check finds them.
    • They forget git rebase --continue: git status says “rebase in progress”.
    • An editor tab opens after --continue (it’s the commit message). Tell them to close the tab. If the editor isn’t set, they get vim; see the setup page.
    • They run git pull after being told not to: have them git reflog and reset, as in episode 4. A good chance to show it working.
    • They use --force rather than --force-with-lease. Remind them.
    • git merge --ff-only refuses: their main has commits of its own. git reset --hard origin/main first (then redo the fast-forward).
    • The one failing test after the rebase isn’t a mistake: it is the hook for episode 10. Don’t explain it yet.

    If someone is hopelessly stuck: git rebase --abort, and give them the resolved peaks.py from the solution, or have a helper pair with them.

    Bridge to episode 10: “We have one failing test, and it isn’t in our code. What changed?”

    Key Points
    • A fast-forward just moves a label, so main stays a straight line
    • Merge joins two tips with a merge commit. Rebase moves your branch’s base, and replays your commits as new ones
    • A conflict means both sides changed the same lines. Resolve it by editing the result to contain what you want. The VS Code merge editor makes this easy
    • In a rebase, “Current” is the branch you’re rebasing onto and “Incoming” is your commit
    • After a rebase, push with --force-with-lease. Never follow git’s hint to git pull
    • Only rewrite history that nobody else is depending on
    • For pull requests, “Rebase and merge” keeps your curated commits and a straight history

    Content from Tracking Down a Bug: Blame and Bisect

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Which commit last changed this line, and what was it for?
    • When did this test start failing?
    • How do I fix a bug I find, without tangling the fix into my own feature?

    Objectives

    • Use blame in VS Code to see which commit changed a line
    • Use git bisect to find the commit where a test started failing
    • Fix a bug on a separate branch, merge it into main, and rebase your feature onto the result

    One test is failing

    At the end of the last episode we rebased onto main and one test failed. It isn’t in our code. Run it again:

    BASH 

    pytest tests/test_normalise.py

    OUTPUT 

    >       assert np.allclose(result, [0, 0.5, 1])
E       assert False
E        +  where False = <function allclose at 0x769723b210b0>(array([-1. , -0.6, -0.2]), [0, 0.5, 1])

    normalise([1, 3, 5]) should give [0, 0.5, 1], but it gives [-1, -0.6, -0.2]. This test passed at v0.1.0, so something changed in the colleague’s six commits that affects it. Two questions: which commit changed normalise, and when did the test start failing?

    Which commit changed this line? Blame

    Open peakfinder/normalise.py in VS Code. The suspicious line is in the range branch. git blame tells you which commit last changed each line, and its author, so you know where to look and who to ask about what the change was for.

    In VS Code:

    1. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac).
    2. Run Git: Toggle Git Blame Editor Decoration. Each line now shows its commit at the end. (Git: Toggle Git Blame Status Bar Item shows the commit for the current line in the status bar instead.)
    3. Hover over the blame text to see the commit hash, message and author.

    On the command line, the same information is:

    BASH 

    git blame -L 5,12 peakfinder/normalise.py

    OUTPUT 

    e2c75380 (Robin Researcher 2025-02-04 11:00:00 +0000  5)     """Scale y. mode is 'range' (0 to 1), 'max' (divide by max) or 'area'."""
b8055cf7 (Sam Scientist    2025-01-06 12:00:00 +0000  6)     y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
e2c75380 (Robin Researcher 2025-02-04 11:00:00 +0000  7)     if mode == "range":
e2c75380 (Robin Researcher 2025-02-04 11:00:00 +0000  8)         return (y - y.min()) / y.max() - y.min()
...

    The suspicious line 8 comes from e2c75380. (-L 5,12 means lines 5 to 12.)

    Callout

    Other ways to look at history

    • Blame isn’t proof. It shows only the last change to a line. A later commit that merely re-indented the code would hide the real change. For when something broke, use bisect, below.
    • The Timeline view (in the Explorer sidebar, for the open file) lists the commits that changed it. The Source Control Graph lists the commits on your branch: select one to see its files, and a file to see the diff.
    • git log -S"text" -- <file> lists the commits that added or removed some text, and git log -L :<function>:<file> shows the history of one function.
    • The GitLens and Git History extensions add richer inline blame and file history, if you like them.

    Bisect: find when it broke

    Blame told us who last touched the line. What we really want is the first commit where the test fails, and git can find that for us, quickly. You know a commit where the test passed (v0.1.0) and one where it fails (main). git bisect does a binary search between them: it checks out the commit in the middle, tests it, and halves the range again.

    flowchart LR
    accTitle: {Bisect narrows seven commits down to the first bad one}
    accDescr: {Seven commits in order from oldest to newest. The oldest, v0.1.0, is known good, shown in green. The newest, Document Peak, is known bad, shown in red. Bisect tests the middle commit first, Remove import, which is bad. It then tests Add mode option, which is bad, and then Fix typo, which is good. So Add mode option is the first bad commit.}
    A["v0.1.0<br/>GOOD"] --> B["Fix typo<br/>test 3: good"] --> C["Add mode option<br/>test 2: bad<br/>FIRST BAD"] --> D["Remove import<br/>test 1: bad"] --> E["Bump version"] --> F["Return Peak"] --> G["Document Peak<br/>BAD"]
    classDef good fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    classDef bad fill:#fdd,stroke:#c00,color:#000
    class A,B good
    class C,D,G bad

    Time runs left to right. With six commits to check it takes three tests. With 1,000 commits, it takes about ten.

    Even better, if the test can be run by a command, git can do the whole search by itself. The command should exit with 0 for “good” and non-zero for “bad”, which is exactly what pytest does:

    BASH 

    git bisect start main v0.1.0
git bisect run pytest -q tests/test_normalise.py
git bisect reset

    (git bisect start <bad> <good>: first the bad commit, then the good one. Always finish with git bisect reset, which puts you back on your own branch.)

    OUTPUT 

    e2c7538061b16250b842ab506cac3c2ae25b20c2 is the first bad commit
commit e2c7538061b16250b842ab506cac3c2ae25b20c2
Author: Robin Researcher <robin.researcher@example.org>

    Add mode option to normalise
...
bisect found first bad commit
    Callout

    By hand: what bisect run is doing

    Without run, you do the testing yourself. Your instructor will show this on screen:

    BASH 

    git bisect start main v0.1.0       # git checks out a commit in the middle
pytest -q tests/test_normalise.py  # it fails...
git bisect bad                     # ...so tell git
pytest -q tests/test_normalise.py  # git moved to an older commit. It fails too...
git bisect bad
pytest -q tests/test_normalise.py  # older still. This one passes
git bisect good                    # git: "... is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset

    At each step you’re on a detached HEAD (episode 2): not on any branch. That’s fine, as git bisect reset puts you back.

    Callout

    Why atomic commits matter here

    Bisect names a commit. If that commit is small and atomic (“Add mode option to normalise”), you know almost exactly where the problem is. If it were a huge commit that changed 900 lines across ten files, bisect would tell you only that the problem is somewhere in there. This is the payoff of episode 3.

    Challenge

    Challenge: find the commit

    1. Run the three commands above to find the commit where test_normalise_runs_from_zero_to_one starts to fail.
    2. Open that commit (git show <hash>, or select it in the Source Control Graph). What exactly is wrong with the range line?
    3. Check you’re back on your feature branch: git branch --show-current.
    1. The first bad commit is Add mode option to normalise.
    2. In range mode, the code is (y - y.min()) / y.max() - y.min(). The brackets are wrong: it divides by y.max() only, and then subtracts y.min(). It should divide by (y.max() - y.min()). It only gives the right answer when the minimum is zero. The existing test would have caught it, but it looks as though the tests weren’t run, and nothing runs them automatically. (That is what we’ll fix in episode 12.)
    3. git bisect reset returns you to your branch.

    If git bisect complains about local changes, you have uncommitted work. Stash it (see the reference page) or commit it, and try again.

    Fix it, but not here

    We know what’s wrong, and the fix is one line. The tempting thing is to fix it on the feature branch, as it’s right there. Don’t. The fix has nothing to do with your feature, so your pull request would mix two ideas. And if the fix is tangled up with your feature, nobody can use it without taking your feature too. We’ll need exactly that in episode 13.

    So put the fix on its own branch from main:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git switch -c fix/normalise

    Fix the line in peakfinder/normalise.py:

    PYTHON 

            return (y - y.min()) / (y.max() - y.min())

    Check it, and commit it with a message that explains why:

    BASH 

    pytest
git commit -am "Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero" -m "The division only applied to y.max(), not to (y.max() - y.min())."

    On a real team you would open a pull request for this fix, and we’ll look at doing that well in the next episode. To keep moving, we’ll merge it straight into main now. Nothing has happened on main since we branched, so git can fast-forward it (episode 9):

    BASH 

    git switch main
git merge --ff-only fix/normalise
git push
git branch -d fix/normalise

    OUTPUT 

    Updating 1c13652..05c314d
Fast-forward
 peakfinder/normalise.py | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

    Finally, your feature branch is based on a main that still has the bug. Rebase it again, as we did in the last episode:

    BASH 

    git switch feature-prominence        # or feature-widths
git rebase main
pytest
git push --force-with-lease

    OUTPUT 

    Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature-prominence.
9 passed

    This time there is no conflict, because the fix touched different lines from your feature, and every test passes.

    Challenge

    Challenge: fix the bug on its own branch

    Do the whole thing yourself:

    1. Create fix/normalise from main, fix the bug, and commit it with a good message.
    2. Fast-forward main to it, push, and delete the branch.
    3. Rebase your feature branch onto the updated main, and push with --force-with-lease.
    4. Check: pytest passes everything, and git log --oneline -5 on your feature branch shows the fix underneath your three commits.

    BASH 

    git switch main
git switch -c fix/normalise
# edit normalise.py: (y - y.min()) / (y.max() - y.min())
pytest
git commit -am "Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero"

git switch main
git merge --ff-only fix/normalise
git push
git branch -d fix/normalise
git switch feature-prominence
git rebase main
pytest
git push --force-with-lease

    OUTPUT 

    ab0c4ef Test min_prominence
b70cf77 Add min_prominence option to find_peaks
6eaff85 Add prominence function
b676f77 Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero
1c13652 Document Peak in the README

    (Your hashes will be different.)

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    1. When might git blame point you at the wrong commit?
    2. Why does git bisect work best with small, atomic commits?
    3. Why did we fix the bug on a separate branch, and not on the feature branch?
    1. When a later commit changed the line without changing what it does, such as re-indenting, renaming a variable or reformatting. Blame shows only the last change, not the one that introduced the bug. (git blame -w ignores whitespace changes, and the VS Code setting git.blame.ignoreWhitespace does the same.)
    2. It names a single commit. If the commit is small and has one purpose, you know where the bug is. A giant commit leaves you searching inside it.
    3. A fix is a separate idea. Mixing it into the feature would give reviewers two things to understand at once, and anyone who wanted just the fix would have to take the feature too.

    Plan (about 30 minutes). Roughly: 3 for the failing test and blame, 7 for bisect (you explain and show the by-hand version, then they run bisect run), 15 for the fix, merge and rebase. If it runs long, trim in this order: the by-hand demo, the -S/-L callout, then the Knowledge check.

    Bisect has two layers. Show the by-hand version once, briefly, so the idea of “binary search” lands. Then learners only type the three-line bisect run, which takes seconds.

    No pull request here, by design. The fix goes straight into main with a fast-forward, which keeps this episode short and saves the pull request mechanics for episode 11. Say out loud that a real team would open one.

    Common problems:

    • git bisect refuses, because of uncommitted changes. Stash or commit.
    • They forget git bisect reset, and wonder why they’re on a detached HEAD. git bisect reset fixes it.
    • They give git the arguments the wrong way round (git bisect start v0.1.0 main): bad first, then good. The result will be nonsense. git bisect reset and again.
    • Bisecting the whole test suite rather than tests/test_normalise.py: other failures can confuse it.
    • No v0.1.0 tag. Their fork has no tags. git tag shows what’s there. They can fetch tags from the original repository, or pair up.
    • git merge --ff-only refuses. main has moved, or they committed the fix on the wrong branch. git status, git log --oneline --graph, and check they branched from main.
    • git branch -d fix/normalise fails with “not fully merged”. The merge didn’t happen, or they’re on the wrong branch.
    • A conflict in the second rebase: it shouldn’t happen. It means they changed normalise.py in their feature branch.

    Bridge to episode 11: “Your feature is ready, on top of a working main. Time to ask your partner to review it.”

    Key Points
    • Blame shows which commit last changed each line (in VS Code: Git: Toggle Git Blame Editor Decoration). It shows only the last change, so it isn’t proof of the cause
    • git bisect binary-searches history for the first commit where a test fails. git bisect run <command> automates it. Always finish with git bisect reset
    • Fix bugs you find on a branch of their own, so the fix is a single idea that can be reviewed and reused

    Content from Pull Requests: Authoring and Reviewing

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What makes a pull request easy to review?
    • How do I give a review that helps?
    • How do I change a pull request after feedback without confusing the reviewer?

    Objectives

    • Check your own branch the way a reviewer will, before you open a pull request
    • Write a pull request description that a reviewer will thank you for
    • Review a pull request one commit at a time, and leave comments that help
    • Respond to feedback with --fixup commits, then autosquash before merging
    • Check that tidying your history didn’t change the code (in VS Code, or with git diff)

    A pull request is a story

    A pull request asks for your branch to be merged. But it is more than a button. It is the place where your work is read by another person, where automatic checks run (episode 12), and where the decision to merge is made.

    When you open one, you are handing someone a small story: “Here is a change, here is why, here is how it was made.” Everything we have done so far, planning, atomic commits and a tidy history, exists to make that story easy to read.

    A reviewer can read it in two ways:

    • all at once, in the Files changed tab, which is one big diff
    • one commit at a time, in the Commits tab, where each commit tells one part of the story

    The second way is far easier, and it only works if your commits are atomic and well named. That is the payoff for the work we did on day 1.

    Here is the life of a pull request, which is what we’ll do in this episode:

    flowchart LR
    accTitle: {The life of a pull request}
    accDescr: {Open the pull request after reviewing your own branch. Your partner reviews it commit by commit. If they leave comments, you push a fixup commit and they review again. When they approve, you squash the fixups with autosquash, and then merge with Rebase and merge.}
    A["Open the PR<br/>(review your own<br/>branch first)"] --> B["Partner reviews<br/>commit by commit"]
    B -->|comments| C["You push a<br/>fixup commit"]
    C --> B
    B -->|approved| D["Squash the fixups<br/>(autosquash)"]
    D --> E["Rebase<br/>and merge"]
    classDef done fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    class E done

    Today we’ll go as far as the approval. Squashing and merging are the last step, and you can do them now or later.

    Before you open it: review your own branch

    The cheapest review is your own. Before you ask anyone else, look at your branch as they will. Go through these:

    Write a description a reviewer will thank you for

    The title and description are the first things a reviewer reads. Tell them what they need to know:

    • What changed, in a sentence or two
    • Why: the problem it solves
    • How to check it: the commands they can run, or what to look at
    • Anything they should pay particular attention to, or that you aren’t sure about

    For our prominence feature, that might be:

    Add a min_prominence option to find_peaks

Our example data has 71 "peaks" and only three real ones, because noise makes lots of
little bumps. A peak's prominence is how far it stands out above the surrounding
valleys, so a minimum prominence removes the bumps on the slope of a real peak.

Three commits: the prominence helper, the new option, and a test. Read them in order.

To check it, run `pytest`. The new test is `test_min_prominence_ignores_bumps_on_a_slope`.

Not sure about: how this should behave for flat-topped peaks.
    Callout

    Pull request templates

    Some repositories have a pull request template: a file called .github/pull_request_template.md that pre-fills the description box with headings (what changed, why, how to test, a checklist). If you see text already in the box when you open a pull request, that’s why. Fill it in rather than deleting it. A project without one can add its own, and it’s a good way for a team to agree what a description should contain.

    Draft pull requests

    If your work isn’t ready but you want early feedback, or you want automatic checks to run, open it as a draft (the arrow on the green button). Nobody will merge it by accident, and you can mark it Ready for review when it is.

    Open the pull request

    1. Push your branch: git push. (It’s already on GitHub from day 1, so this should say everything is up to date.)
    2. On GitHub, open your fork, and click Compare & pull request next to your branch. (Or Pull requests, then New pull request.)
    3. Check the base repository. It must be your own fork (YOUR-USERNAME/peakfinder), with base branch main. Use the base repository dropdown to change it if needed. (See the warning below.)
    4. Write the title and description. Click Create pull request.
    5. In the right-hand sidebar, ask your partner for a review: Reviewers, then choose their username.

    Look at the Commits tab. Each of your commits is there, one at a time. That’s what your reviewer will use.

    Callout

    Make sure the pull request is on your fork

    Pull requests from a fork default to the project you forked from. If you create one against the original, you will be sending it to the course repository. Check the “base repository” line at the top of the page before you press the button. It should show your own username. From here on, every pull request in this workshop is on your own fork.

    Giving a good review

    Now swap. Your partner has opened a pull request in their fork. Open it (they’ll send you the link, or it will be in your notifications).

    How to read it

    1. Read the description. Do you know what to expect?
    2. Go to the Commits tab. Read the commits one at a time, from the oldest. Does each one do what its message says?
    3. Look at each commit’s diff. Hover over a line in the diff and click the blue + to comment on that line.
    4. Ask yourself: Is this correct? Is it clear? Is anything missing, like a test?

    What good comments look like

    • Be specific. “This loop is hard to follow” is less useful than “Could we name i as index? I had to scroll back to see what it was.”
    • Ask questions rather than giving orders. “What happens for a peak at the edge of the data?” invites a conversation, and might teach you something.
    • Mark the small things. Start optional, minor comments with nit: (short for nitpick) so the author knows they won’t block the merge.
    • Suggest the change. On a line comment, the Add a suggestion button writes your replacement code in the comment, and the author can apply it with one click.
    • Say what’s good. A review that is only complaints is hard to read. If something is neat, say so.
    • Review the code, not the person. “This doesn’t handle…” rather than “You forgot…”

    When you’ve finished, click Review changes (top right of Files changed) and choose:

    Choice Meaning
    Comment feedback only
    Approve looks good to merge
    Request changes something must change first
    Challenge

    Challenge: swap and review

    Review your partner’s pull request, one commit at a time, in the Commits tab. Leave exactly three comments:

    1. one nit: (short for nitpick: a small thing the author could improve)
    2. one question
    3. one suggestion, using the Add a suggestion button

    Then submit the review as Comment (we’ll approve it in a moment).

    No partner, or your partner isn’t ready? Review the example pull request your instructor shares instead.

    Need an idea for something to comment on? Good first things to look at are the docstring of the helper function in the first commit, the names of variables in it, and what the test doesn’t cover (flat peaks, peaks at the edges, an empty list).

    Responding to feedback

    You’ve got a review, and you want to change something in an earlier commit, such as the docstring in your first commit. There are three common ways to do it, and each has a cost:

    Approach What you do Easy for the reviewer? History afterwards The catch
    “Address review” commits Add new commits on the end, e.g. PR: rename variable, and push normally Yes: each new commit is exactly what changed Messy, unless the pull request is squash-merged Fine if your team squash-merges anyway, because the commits vanish
    Fixup commits, squashed before merging git commit --fixup <hash>, push normally. When approved, autosquash and --force-with-lease Yes: same as above Clean Someone has to autosquash before the merge. GitHub’s merge buttons won’t do it for you, so you tell the reviewer
    Amend and force-push every round Fix the commit in place, --force-with-lease No: new hashes everywhere, so they re-read everything Clean Easy to lose track of what changed. Comments become “outdated”

    Our recommendation: fixup commits, squashed when it’s approved. It’s the only one that is easy to review and leaves a clean history. The cost is one short bit of coordination: you say “approved, so I’m squashing the fixups now. The code won’t change, and I’ll check that.” If your team squash-merges every pull request, ignore all this: plain “address review” commits are fine, since the history is flattened anyway.

    For a fixup, the steps are what you did yesterday, with one difference: you push it normally, with no force, because you only added a commit.

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..          # find the hash of the commit it belongs to
git commit --fixup <hash>
git push

    OUTPUT 

       ab0c4ef..9ae8b33  feature-prominence -> feature-prominence

    Your reviewer opens the pull request and sees one small commit, fixup! Add prominence function, which contains exactly your change. There’s nothing to re-read.

    Challenge

    Challenge: respond and approve

    1. Address one of the comments you received, as a fixup of the commit it belongs to. Stage it in VS Code, then git commit --fixup <hash> in the terminal, and push it (a normal push).
    2. Reply to the comment: “Done, in <hash>.”
    3. As the reviewer, look at your partner’s fixup commit in the Commits tab. It should be small and obvious. If it’s right, approve their pull request: Review changes, then Approve.

    BASH 

    git log --oneline main..
git add -u                                  # or stage in the Source Control view
git commit --fixup <hash-of-the-first-commit>
git push

    Then reply on GitHub, and your partner approves from the Review changes button.

    Finishing: squash and merge

    When your pull request is approved, say so in a comment and tidy the history before merging. Do this now if there’s time, or later.

    BASH 

    git rebase -i --autosquash main

    Your fixup folds into the commit it belongs to, and the commits get new hashes. Before you push, check that nothing but the history changed:

    • In VS Code: in the Source Control Graph, right-click your newest commit and choose Compare with Remote. It compares your tidied branch with the version on GitHub, the one your reviewer approved. It should list no changed files.
    • On the command line: git diff @{u} HEAD should print nothing. (@{u} means “the branch on GitHub that this one tracks”.)

    Then push the tidy version, safely (episode 9), and merge:

    BASH 

    git push --force-with-lease

    On GitHub, merge with Rebase and merge. Then update your local main:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git pull

    (For a per-commit comparison of the old and new series there is also git range-diff @{u}...HEAD, but the check above is usually all you need.)

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    1. After autosquashing, git diff @{u} HEAD prints nothing, yet every commit has a new hash. How can both be true?
    2. When are plain “address review” commits a perfectly good choice?
    1. A diff compares files, and the files are identical. The commits are different, because squashing the fixup rewrote them (episode 2: a changed commit, or a changed parent, means a new hash). Same code, tidier history.
    2. When your team squash-merges every pull request. The commits are flattened into one anyway, so how tidy they were makes no difference.

    Timing (about 30 minutes). 12 minutes of talk, then the exercises in time-boxes: open the pull request (4), review (8), respond and approve (6). Use a visible timer. Review takes longest, so don’t let it overrun: three comments only. The Finishing section (squash and merge) is optional in the session: say it’s there for when they have time, or to do later. (Learners who don’t merge won’t be affected: nothing in the later episodes needs this feature merged.)

    The base repository trap. Check screens as people open their pull requests. Anything opened against the course repository should be closed and re-opened on the fork.

    Pairs. Make sure each learner has been added as a collaborator (episode 1), and the invitation accepted: they need it to be asked for a review. If a partner is missing or behind, pair them with a helper, or have them review the instructor’s example pull request.

    Online. Breakout rooms of two. Ask people to share the pull request link in the chat or room.

    Common problems:

    • The pull request is against the course repository. Close it and open a new one on the fork.
    • The reviewer can’t find the pull request. Send the link. Check notification emails.
    • They git commit --fixup the wrong commit. The autosquash puts the change in the wrong place. git rebase --abort, or fix it with another interactive rebase.
    • They squash before the reviewer has looked and then wonder where their comments went. GitHub keeps them, marked “outdated”.
    • No partner. Use the prepared example pull request. Have one ready on your own fork, with a few things to comment on.
    • git diff @{u} HEAD isn’t empty. Something else changed. Look at it with git diff @{u} HEAD --stat.
    • @{u} means nothing, or errors: the branch has no upstream. git push -u origin <branch> sets it.
    • @{u} in some shells needs quoting ('@{u}'). In Git Bash it works as is.
    • After merging, the branch still shows in the list. There is a Delete branch button on the merged pull request.

    What to point out: that every commit and every comment they wrote on day 1 and now is the thing the reviewer is reading. A reviewer who can follow the story approves faster.

    Key Points
    • A pull request is a story. Review your own first: it should read well, each commit should pass, it should be up to date and contain only your change
    • Write a description that says what, why, and how to check it
    • Review one commit at a time. Be specific, ask questions, mark small things with nit:, suggest changes, and say what’s good
    • Respond to feedback with --fixup commits that you push as they are, and autosquash when it’s approved (say so first). If your team squash-merges, plain “address review” commits are fine
    • git diff @{u} HEAD printing nothing (or Compare with Remote in VS Code showing no files) proves that tidying the history didn’t change the code
    • Use Rebase and merge to keep your curated commits and a straight history
    • A pull request from a fork defaults to the original repository, so check the base repository is your own fork

    Content from Catching Problems Early: Shift Left and CI

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 26 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I catch problems before a reviewer has to?
    • What does “shift left” mean, and which checks belong where?
    • What is continuous integration, and how do I set it up with GitHub Actions?

    Objectives

    • Explain “shift left”, and say where different kinds of check belong
    • Describe pre-commit hooks and their trade-offs
    • Read a GitHub Actions workflow, add one that runs the tests on every pull request, and read a failing run

    The bug nobody ran a test for

    In episode 10 we found a bug in the colleague’s commit. There was already a test that caught it. It failed the moment the change was made. It just wasn’t run.

    We can’t rely on everyone remembering to run every check, every time, and a reviewer shouldn’t have to find problems a machine could. So let’s think about where each kind of check belongs.

    Shift left

    Picture a change moving from left to right, from the moment you type it to the moment users have it. At each stage, a problem can be noticed, but the later it’s noticed, the longer you wait to find out and the more it costs to fix.

    flowchart LR
    accTitle: {Six stages a change passes through, and how long it takes to find a problem at each}
    accDescr: {From left to right: 1, in your editor, you find out as you type, instantly. 2, in a pre-commit hook, when you commit, in seconds. 3, running the tests yourself before you push, in seconds or minutes. 4, continuous integration after you push, in a few minutes. 5, code review, in hours or days. 6, released to users, in weeks. Problems are cheap to fix on the left and expensive on the right.}
    A["<b>1. Editor</b><br/>as you type<br/>(instant)"] --> B["<b>2. Pre-commit</b><br/>when you commit<br/>(seconds)"] --> C["<b>3. Your tests</b><br/>before you push<br/>(seconds to minutes)"] --> D["<b>4. CI</b><br/>after you push<br/>(minutes)"] --> E["<b>5. Review</b><br/>(hours to days)"] --> F["<b>6. Users</b><br/>after release<br/>(weeks)"]
    classDef cheap fill:#dfd,stroke:#080,color:#000
    classDef mid fill:#ffd,stroke:#a80,color:#000
    classDef dear fill:#fdd,stroke:#c00,color:#000
    class A,B,C cheap
    class D,E mid
    class F dear

    Green: cheap and fast to fix. Red: slow and expensive. Time runs left to right.

    “Shift left” means moving each check as far left as it sensibly can go. The rule of thumb is to push a check left until it becomes too slow or too annoying to run there:

    Stage What belongs there Why
    1. Editor formatting, lint warnings, typos, type errors instant, and you never see them again
    2. Pre-commit the same fast checks, enforced optional, and only if it stays fast
    3. Before you push the tests too slow for every keystroke, but cheap to run now and then
    4. CI the tests again, on a clean machine, plus slower checks (other Python versions, building the docs) nobody can skip it
    5. Review design, naming, “is this the right change?” the things only a person can judge

    So formatting goes as far left as it can: set up your editor so it’s fixed before you ever commit. The tests are slower and more costly, so you run them yourself before pushing, and CI runs them for everyone, regardless. The point of the earlier stages is that review, and the users, only get to see changes that have already passed everything a machine can check.

    Stage 1: your editor

    The earliest check is the one you don’t have to think about. A linter finds likely mistakes without running your program, such as unused imports, undefined names and unreachable code. A formatter fixes layout. ruff is a fast tool that does both for Python, and the Ruff extension for VS Code shows its findings as you type and can format when you save (turn on Format on Save in VS Code’s settings).

    On the command line, you can ask it the same question. In the original peakfinder, it finds the unused import sys that the colleague later removed:

    BASH 

    ruff check .

    OUTPUT 

    F401 [*] `sys` imported but unused
 --> peakfinder/cli.py:2:8
  |
1 | import argparse
2 | import sys
  |        ^^^
  |
help: Remove unused import: `sys`

    This is the cheapest feedback there is, and it needs no workshop to set up. (How you configure these tools varies between projects, so look at what yours uses.)

    Stage 2: pre-commit hooks

    Git can run a script just before each commit, called a hook. The pre-commit tool manages these for you. You list the checks in a .pre-commit-config.yaml file:

    YAML 

    repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
    rev: <a version>        # `pre-commit autoupdate` fills in the latest
    hooks:
      - id: ruff

    Each person runs pip install pre-commit and pre-commit install once. From then on, git commit runs the checks on the files you’re committing, and refuses to commit if one fails.

    Pros Cons
    Finds problems in seconds, before they’re committed Every contributor has to install it, and it is not on by default
    Keeps everyone’s formatting the same Slow hooks interrupt every commit
    Can fix things automatically (formatting) Gets in the way of messy work-in-progress commits, which we may want to make and tidy up later
    Can be skipped: git commit --no-verify

    Opinions differ, and several of us find hooks more annoying than helpful. If you like them, use them and keep the hooks fast (formatting and linting, not the whole test suite). Never rely on them alone, because they can be skipped.

    Stage 3: run the tests before you push

    Nothing clever here: run pytest before you push. For a quick check of every commit on your branch (not just the last), as we did in episode 7:

    BASH 

    git rebase main --exec "pytest -q"

    It stops at the first commit where the tests fail. That’s how you confirm each commit is atomic, with the tests passing at every step.

    Stage 4: continuous integration

    You can skip any of the stages above, and sometimes you will. Continuous integration (CI) is the one you can’t skip, so it’s the backstop for everything. Every time someone proposes a change, a computer automatically builds the project and runs the checks, on a clean machine, and reports back.

    • A reviewer sees a green tick or a red cross on the pull request, before they’ve read a line.
    • It runs in a fresh environment, so “it works on my machine” can’t hide a missing dependency.
    • It runs every time, whether or not anyone remembers.

    GitHub Actions is GitHub’s built-in way to do this, and it’s free for public repositories. You describe what to run in a workflow file, a small YAML file in the .github/workflows/ folder of your repository:

    YAML 

    name: Tests                          # what this workflow is called

on:                                  # WHEN to run it
  pull_request:                      #   on every pull request
  push:
    branches: [main]                 #   and on every push to main

jobs:
  test:                              # a job: a list of steps on one machine
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest           # GitHub gives us a fresh Linux machine
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7    # use a ready-made action: get our code

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
          cache: pip

      - name: Install the requirements
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt   # run a command

      - name: Run the tests
        run: pytest

    Read it from the top: when it runs (on), where (runs-on), then the steps. A step either uses a ready-made action, or runs a command. The commands are the ones you’d type yourself: the same pip install and pytest as in our setup page.

    Callout

    YAML is fussy

    YAML uses indentation to show structure. Use spaces, never tabs, and keep the indentation exactly as shown. A step that’s one space out will fail with a confusing error. VS Code shows the indentation guides, which helps.

    Add CI, and watch it catch a mistake

    We’ll do this in one pull request: add the workflow, see it go green, then make a plausible mistake and watch CI catch it. The mistake is renaming something in the code but forgetting to update its test, and pushing without running the tests. (We’re skipping stage 3 on purpose. In real life, it happens by accident.)

    Challenge

    Challenge: add CI, then break it and fix it

    Your fork needs Actions switched on. Open the Actions tab of your fork. If it offers a button saying “I understand my workflows, go ahead and enable them”, click it. (You did this in the setup. This is where we find out if it worked.)

    Callout

    If Actions won’t run for you

    GitHub Actions is the one part of today that depends on GitHub doing something at the right moment, and sometimes it’s slow, or switched off. If your checks don’t appear or you’re stuck waiting, don’t wait. Watch the instructor’s prepared run on screen, and carry on with the git steps, which are the same either way: the commits, the fixup and the autosquash all work without Actions. You’ll still see the point of CI.

    Part 1: add the workflow.

    1. Update main and make a branch:

      BASH 

      git switch main
git pull
git switch -c add-ci

    2. Create the file .github/workflows/tests.yml (in VS Code: create a folder .github, with a folder workflows inside it, and a file tests.yml) containing the workflow above.

    3. Commit it with a clear message, and push:

      BASH 

      git add .github/workflows/tests.yml
git commit -m "Run the tests on every pull request"
git push

    4. Open a pull request in your own fork (check the base repository!) from add-ci into main.

    5. Scroll to the bottom of the pull request. In the checks section, you’ll see your Tests job running (a yellow dot), then a green tick. Click Details to read the log, which shows each step.

    Part 2: break it, on the same pull request.

    1. In peakfinder/normalise.py, rename the mode "max" to "maximum" (the line if mode == "max":). Only the code. Commit and push, without running pytest:

      BASH 

      git commit -am "Rename the normalise mode 'max' to 'maximum'"
git push

    2. Go back to the pull request. The checks run again, and this time they fail: a red cross. Click Details, open the Run the tests step, and find the error. Is it the same as you would see locally?

    Part 3: fix it where it belongs, and merge.

    1. The test should have been part of the same commit. In tests/test_normalise.py, change mode="max" to mode="maximum", then make it a fixup of the rename commit, and tidy up:

      BASH 

      git log --oneline -3
git add -u
git commit --fixup <hash of the rename commit>
git rebase -i --autosquash main
git push --force-with-lease

    2. Watch the pull request: the checks run again, and go green.

    3. Merge it with Rebase and merge (the rename is harmless, so we’ll keep it), then update your local main: git switch main, then git pull.

    If the job doesn’t start at all, check the Actions tab is enabled, and that the file is in exactly .github/workflows/.

    The workflow file is the one on this page. The finished steps:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git pull
git switch -c add-ci
# create .github/workflows/tests.yml
git add .github/workflows/tests.yml
git commit -m "Run the tests on every pull request"
git push
# open the pull request on GitHub (base: your fork's main). Wait for the tick

# edit normalise.py: if mode == "max" -> "maximum"
git commit -am "Rename the normalise mode 'max' to 'maximum'"
git push                                  # CI runs, and fails

# edit tests/test_normalise.py: mode="max" -> mode="maximum"
git log --oneline -3
git add -u
git commit --fixup <hash of the rename commit>
git rebase -i --autosquash main
git push --force-with-lease               # CI runs again, and passes

# Rebase and merge on GitHub, then
git switch main
git pull

    In step 7 the log shows:

    OUTPUT 

    FAILED tests/test_normalise.py::test_normalise_max_mode - ValueError: unknown mode: max
1 failed, 7 passed

    which is exactly what pytest would print on your own computer. After the autosquash, the pull request has two commits, each one passing: the workflow, and the rename with its test. The fixup workflow kept the mistake out of the history.

    OUTPUT 

    28171b1 Rename the normalise mode 'max' to 'maximum'
7ba3c1f Run the tests on every pull request

    (Your hashes will be different.)

    Going further: more checks in CI

    A good CI job is the list of things you’d want a careful reviewer to check by hand. The linter from stage 1 is easy to add. Append one more step (indented to match the others):

    YAML 

          - name: Check the code for common mistakes
        run: |
          pip install ruff
          ruff check .

    The same idea works for formatting (ruff format --check .), type checks, and building the documentation. Anything that’s too slow to run in your editor, but worth running on every change, belongs here.

    How this connects to history

    CI and everything else we have learned reinforce each other:

    • Each commit should pass, but CI usually only checks the tip. The rename commit failed CI because its test was missing, and we fixed it in the commit, so every commit passes. git rebase main --exec "pytest -q" checks all of them.
    • Bisect uses the same test command. CI keeps the commands you’d bisect with working.
    • Merging can be made conditional. Repositories can require the checks to pass before the merge button works (Settings, then Rules or Branches). Then a failing change can’t reach main, even by accident.
    • The reviewer sees the result. A green tick means they can spend their time on the design, which is the one thing only they can do.
    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    Where would you put each of these checks, and why?

    1. Fixing the formatting of your code
    2. A test suite that takes ten minutes
    3. Running the tests on three different versions of Python
    4. Deciding whether a function has a good name
    1. Your editor (format on save): it’s instant, and you never see the problem again.
    2. CI, and run a quick subset yourself before you push. A ten-minute check on every commit would be painful, but CI can run it in the background while you carry on.
    3. CI. You’d rarely have three versions of Python to hand locally, and CI can run them in parallel on clean machines.
    4. Code review. Only a person can judge it, and it’s what review is for.

    Timing (about 26 minutes). Talk for 10: the table of stages is the key idea, and the stage 2 and 3 sections can be quick. Then the single challenge, which has just one pull request for both exercises.
