Start the CI pull request early and talk while it runs: the first run takes up to a minute, and there’s waiting time in the exercise. If you’re short on time, do part 1 together, then do part 2 and 3 (break and fix) as a demonstration on your screen. The “going further” step is talking only.

    Emphasise the principle: push each check left until it’s too slow or annoying. Ask the room: “what do you already run before pushing?”

    Test this before the workshop. I could check the workflow with actionlint and its commands in a clean environment, but not run it on GitHub. Do the whole exercise on a real fork the day before. Also re-check the versions of actions/checkout and actions/setup-python.

    Actions must be enabled on each fork (setup page, step 6). Ask for a show of hands before you start. The Actions tab shows an enable button if not.

    Common problems:

    • Nothing happens on the pull request. Actions is disabled on the fork, or the file isn’t in .github/workflows/, or the pull request is on the course repository instead of the fork.
    • The workflow fails with a YAML error. Indentation, or a tab. Open the Actions tab and read the error.
    • “Rebase and merge” is greyed out. The branch isn’t up to date, or the repository setting is off. Check Settings then General then Pull Requests.
    • The test doesn’t fail in the break-and-fix. They renamed the string in the test as well. Start again.
    • After the autosquash the push is rejected: use --force-with-lease.

    Prepare a fallback before the session. Actions is the part most likely to slow the room down (it runs on GitHub, so you can’t control the timing). Have these ready:

    • A prepared fork with the add-ci pull request already open: a green run, and then the breaking commit with a red run, and a link to each. (Or screenshots of each stage if you can’t rely on the network.)
    • A decision made in advance about when to stop waiting. A sensible rule: if checks haven’t appeared after two minutes, you screenshare the prepared run and move on.
    • Three levels of fallback, from best to simplest: (1) learners run it themselves; (2) learners do the git steps, and you demonstrate the Actions results on your screen; (3) you explain and demonstrate everything, and learners just read the workflow file. Any of them still teaches the idea.

    Limits. Public repositories get free Actions minutes. If the fork is private, the allowance is limited. Forks of public repositories are public.

    Bridge to episode 13: “We have a fix, merged on main. But users are still running version 0.2, which has the bug. How do we get the fix to them?”

    Key Points
    • “Shift left”: find problems as early, cheaply and quickly as you can. Push each check left until it becomes too slow or annoying to run there
    • Formatting and linting belong in your editor. Tests you run yourself before pushing, and CI runs them again for everyone, plus anything slower
    • Pre-commit hooks are an optional personal convenience, and can be skipped. CI is the shared gate that can’t
    • A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/: when to run, where, and a list of steps
    • Fix a failing check in the commit it belongs to (--fixup, then autosquash), so that every commit passes

    Content from Releases: Versions, Tags and Cherry-pick

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What does the life of a released project look like?
    • How do I mark a release, and fix a bug in a version that’s already out?
    • How do I copy a single commit onto another branch?

    Objectives

    • Describe a simple lifecycle for a released project, and what a version number tells you
    • Explain how a tag differs from HEAD and from a branch
    • Choose between “fix on main and release again” and “patch an old release”
    • Cherry-pick a commit onto a release branch, and tag and push a release

    The life of a released project

    So far we’ve worked towards getting changes into main. But a project doesn’t end there. Here is the simplified life of most software:

    1. You develop on main, through small branches and pull requests.
    2. At some point you release: you pick a version number and mark that commit.
    3. Users run that version, and find bugs.
    4. You fix them on main, and release again.

    In git, that looks like a line of commits with a tag at each release:

    gitGraph
    accTitle: {A project's history with a tag at each release}
    accDescr: {A single line of commits on the main branch, from oldest on the left to newest on the right. Three of the commits carry release tags: v0.1.0, v0.2.0 and v0.3.0. Between the tags are the ordinary commits made while developing.}
    commit id: "First commit"
    commit id: "Add normalise"
    commit id: "Add plotting" tag: "v0.1.0"
    commit id: "Add modes"
    commit id: "Return Peak" tag: "v0.2.0"
    commit id: "Add prominence"
    commit id: "Add widths" tag: "v0.3.0"

    That is the whole model. Bigger projects add more branches and ceremony (you may hear the name git flow), but most research software gets by with this. The one extra wrinkle is what to do when a bug is found in a version that’s already out, which we’ll come to.

    Version numbers

    A release needs a name, and a version number is how people refer to it. Most projects use semantic versioning, three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

    Change Which number goes up Example
    Bug fixes only PATCH 0.2.0 to 0.2.1
    New features that don’t break existing use MINOR 0.2.1 to 0.3.0
    Changes that may break existing use MAJOR 0.3.0 to 1.0.0

    So the version tells a user what to expect before they upgrade: a patch should be safe to take, and a major release may need them to change something.

    Tags: names for releases

    Git needs a way to say “this exact commit is version 0.2.1”, and a tag is that. It helps to compare the three kinds of label git has:

    Label Points at Does it move?
    HEAD where you are right now Yes: every time you switch or commit
    A branch (main, release/0.2) the latest commit of a line of work Yes: every time you commit on it
    A tag (v0.2.1) one specific commit Never: that’s the point

    Because a tag never moves, “version 0.2.1” always means exactly the same code.

    There are two kinds of tag:

    Created with What it is
    Lightweight git tag v0.2.1 just a label on a commit
    Annotated git tag -a v0.2.1 -m "message" a label plus a small object that records who tagged it, when, and a message

    Use annotated tags for releases. git show v0.2.1 shows the message. Two more things to know:

    • Tags aren’t pushed by default. You send one explicitly: git push origin v0.2.1.
    • A tag is on a commit, not a branch. git switch -c release/0.2 v0.2.0 makes a branch that starts at the tagged commit.

    A bug in a released version

    Our version 0.2.0 was released with the normalise bug in it, and people are using it. We’ve fixed the bug on main, but main has moved on since then, and also contains new, unreleased features.

    You have two options, from the lifecycle:

    • Fix on main and release a new version (0.3.0). This is the simplest, and the right answer when users can upgrade. Do this if you can.
    • Make a patch release (0.2.1) of the old version. This is for when users can’t just upgrade: perhaps 0.3.0 changes something they depend on, or it isn’t ready. We want to give them just the fix.

    For the second option, we make a release branch that starts from the old version’s tag, and bring the fix across. We don’t want the whole of main, only that one commit. How do we copy a single commit?

    Cherry-pick

    git cherry-pick <commit> takes one commit from anywhere in the repository and replays its change on top of your current branch, as a new commit. This is the “commit as a change” way of thinking from episode 2: git works out what that commit changed, and applies the same change here.

    BASH 

    git switch <the branch you want to put it on>
git cherry-pick <hash of the commit to copy>
    gitGraph
    accTitle: {A bug fix copied onto a release branch}
    accDescr: {The main branch has the version 0.2.0 release. A release branch for 0.2 is created from that point. Meanwhile main gains new commits, including the fix for the normalise bug, a new feature and more work. The fix is cherry-picked onto the release branch, which is then given a version bump and the tag v0.2.1. The feature and later work stay on main only.}
    commit id: "Release 0.2.0" tag: "v0.2.0"
    branch release/0.2
    checkout main
    commit id: "Fix"
    commit id: "Feature"
    checkout release/0.2
    cherry-pick id: "Fix"
    checkout main
    commit id: "More work"
    checkout release/0.2
    commit id: "Bump version" tag: "v0.2.1"

    It makes a new commit with a new hash, as the parent is different. So the original and the copy are two separate commits with the same change. The option -x records where it came from, in the message:

    (cherry picked from commit 05c314d857072a26b300c8be5ce6a350126c3000)

    That makes it easy to see later that two commits are the same fix. Use -x whenever you cherry-pick onto a shared branch, such as a release.

    Callout

    This only works because of atomic commits

    Our fix is one small commit that does one thing. It can be copied cleanly, and the result is a sensible release.

    If the fix had been bundled into a larger commit along with a new feature, cherry-picking it would drag half the feature along, or fail with conflicts because the feature depends on code the release branch doesn’t have. That’s the episode 3 payoff again: atomic commits are what make cherry-pick safe.

    Callout

    In VS Code

    In the Source Control Graph, right-click a commit and choose Cherry Pick to apply it to the branch you have checked out. (If you can’t see the commit, change which branches the graph is showing.) If there’s a conflict, resolve it in the merge editor as before, then finish with git cherry-pick --continue in the terminal. To give up, run Git: Abort Cherry Pick from the Command Palette, or git cherry-pick --abort.

    Challenge

    Challenge: release the fix as version 0.2.1

    Work in your clone, with your virtual environment active.

    1. Make a release branch and bring the fix across. First find the fix on main: it has the message Fix ‘range’ mode of normalise…. (You deleted your fix/normalise branch, so look it up by its message.) Then branch from the old tag, check the bug is there, and cherry-pick:

    BASH 

    git switch main
git pull
git log --oneline --grep="Fix 'range' mode"

git switch -c release/0.2 v0.2.0
pytest tests/test_normalise.py           # fails: the bug is in 0.2.0
git cherry-pick -x <hash of the fix>
pytest                                   # passes

    2. Bump the version, tag it, and push. Change the version to 0.2.1 in two places, __version__ in peakfinder/__init__.py and version in pyproject.toml (edit them in VS Code). Then:

    BASH 

    git commit -am "Bump version to 0.2.1"
git tag -a v0.2.1 -m "Version 0.2.1: fix the 'range' mode of normalise"
git push -u origin release/0.2 v0.2.1

    3. Check it:

    BASH 

    git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate -8

    You should see v0.2.1 on release/0.2, with the cherry-picked fix just below it, and the new features only on main.

    Optional: publish a GitHub release. On your fork’s page, click Releases, then Create a new release. Choose the tag v0.2.1, click Generate release notes, and then Publish release.

    BASH 

    git switch main
git pull
git log --oneline --grep="Fix 'range' mode"      # note the hash

git switch -c release/0.2 v0.2.0
pytest tests/test_normalise.py                  # fails
git cherry-pick -x <hash>
pytest                                          # passes

# edit __version__ in peakfinder/__init__.py and version in pyproject.toml to 0.2.1
git commit -am "Bump version to 0.2.1"
git tag -a v0.2.1 -m "Version 0.2.1: fix the 'range' mode of normalise"
git push -u origin release/0.2 v0.2.1

    The cherry-pick:

    OUTPUT 

    [release/0.2 9bbd943] Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero
 Author: Sam Scientist <sam.scientist@example.org>
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

    and the picture afterwards (hashes will differ):

    OUTPUT 

    * fe33fcc (HEAD -> release/0.2, tag: v0.2.1, origin/release/0.2) Bump version to 0.2.1
* 9bbd943 Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero
| * 05c314d (origin/main, main) Fix 'range' mode of normalise for spectra that don't start at zero
...
* df97539 (tag: v0.2.0) Bump version to 0.2.0

    The same fix is on both branches, as two different commits. release/0.2 has the fix and none of the new features.

    Callout

    Releases and research software

    A tagged release is what people cite and reproduce. If you link your GitHub repository to Zenodo, every GitHub release gets its own DOI, a permanent citable identifier for exactly that version. A CITATION.cff file in the repository tells people how to cite you. Tags and releases turn “the code I used in the paper” into something others can find.

    Challenge

    Knowledge check

    1. A bug is found in 0.2.0, and 0.3.0 has just been released. Users can upgrade without trouble. Do you need a release branch?
    2. Which of HEAD, a branch and a tag will still point at the same commit tomorrow, whatever you do?
    3. Why does the cherry-picked fix have a different hash from the original?
    4. A teammate cherry-picks a commit that adds a feature, and it fails with a conflict. What is the likely reason?
    1. No. Fix it on main, and release 0.3.1 (or whatever comes next). A release branch is only needed when users can’t move to the new version.
    2. The tag. HEAD and branches move when you switch or commit.
    3. A commit’s hash depends on its parent (and the other contents). The copy sits on a different parent, so it’s a new commit, even though its change is the same. -x records where it came from.
    4. The commit depends on earlier commits that the target branch doesn’t have, such as a helper function the feature uses. A commit that is a self-contained change copies cleanly. That’s why atomic commits matter.

    Timing (about 35 minutes). 15 minutes for the lifecycle, versions, tags and cherry-pick, and 20 for the exercise. The GitHub release is optional, and a good thing to demo while people finish.

    Keep the lifecycle simple. Don’t be drawn into branching-model debates. If someone asks about git flow, say it’s a heavier version of the same idea, for software with scheduled releases, and move on.

    Find the fix by its message. Learners deleted their fix/normalise branch in episode 10, so they look up the commit on main with git log --grep. (The hash is the same one the branch had, but they may not have noted it.)

    Common problems:

    • git cherry-pick says the commit is empty or already applied. They are on main instead of release/0.2. Check git branch --show-current.
    • git switch -c release/0.2 v0.2.0 says the tag doesn’t exist. Their fork has no tags (forked with “Copy the default branch only”). git tag shows what’s there. They can fetch tags from the original repository, or pair up.
    • They forget -x. Harmless here, but explain what it would have told them.
    • A conflict on the cherry-pick. It shouldn’t happen. If it does, they’ve probably edited normalise.py on the release branch. git cherry-pick --abort and start again.
    • They tag with a lightweight tag (no -a). It works, but git tag -n shows no message. Delete it (git tag -d v0.2.1) and re-tag.
    • The tag doesn’t appear on GitHub. They pushed the branch but not the tag. git push origin v0.2.1.
    • No “Create a new release” button. On a fork, check Releases is enabled under Settings.

    Bridge to episode 14: “That’s the whole workflow. A few things to make it quicker.”

    Key Points
    • Most projects follow a loop: develop on main, release with a version number and a tag, fix bugs on main, and release again
    • Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) tells users what to expect from an upgrade
    • A tag is a label that never moves, unlike HEAD and branches. Use annotated tags (git tag -a) for releases, and push them explicitly
    • If users can upgrade, fix on main and release again. If they can’t, patch the old release on a release branch
    • git cherry-pick -x <commit> replays one commit’s change as a new commit, and atomic commits are what make it safe

    Content from Tooling and Wrap-up

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What small things make these habits quicker?
    • Which VS Code features match what we did in the terminal?
    • What should I take away and try on Monday?

    Objectives

    • Create useful git aliases, and know a few settings worth turning on
    • Match the commands from the workshop to VS Code’s source control features
    • Pick one habit to adopt first

    Make the good habits quicker

    This episode is a menu, not a to-do list. Skim it, or read it after the workshop. Everything here is a personal choice.

    An alias is a nickname for a git command. Plenty of people use none at all, and typing the full command is perfectly fine. These are some of the ones that are commonly shared, if you’d like a few:

    BASH 

    git config --global alias.st "status -sb"
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate"
git config --global alias.unstage "restore --staged"
git config --global alias.last "log -1 --stat"
    Type It runs You’d use it to
    git st git status -sb a short status, with the branch
    git lg git log --oneline --graph --decorate see the history as a picture
    git unstage <file> git restore --staged <file> take a file out of the next commit
    git last git log -1 --stat see what the last commit changed

    They’re stored in your ~/.gitconfig file. Change them, add your own, and delete the ones you don’t use. (VS Code covers a lot of this already, so you may not need any.)

    A word on settings

    Git’s defaults are the defaults for good reasons, and a lot of the advice about settings online is one person’s preference. Change a setting when you’ve hit the problem it solves, not before. The three we asked you to set in the setup (pull.rebase, rebase.autoSquash and push.autoSetupRemote) suit the workflow in this workshop, but they are preferences too, and many people never change them.

    If you want to try something, these three are widely recommended and low-risk:

    Setting What it does
    fetch.prune true removes your copies of branches that were deleted on GitHub, so your branch list stays tidy
    rebase.autoStash true stashes uncommitted changes before a rebase, and puts them back afterwards
    merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 conflict markers also show the original version, which makes conflicts easier to understand (needs Git 2.35 or newer)

    Set one with git config --global <setting> <value>, and undo it with git config --global --unset <setting>.

    VS Code and the terminal

    We used both. This table matches what we did to what VS Code offers, so you can use whichever you prefer.

    What we did In VS Code
    Stage part of a file (ep 5) In the diff editor, select lines and use the gutter Stage button, or right-click Stage Selected Ranges
    Unstage, or discard changes the - icon, or right-click Discard Changes
    Amend the last commit (ep 5) the dropdown on the Commit button, then Commit (Amend)
    Undo the last commit (ep 5) ..., then Commit, then Undo Last Commit
    Read your branch like a reviewer (ep 7) the Source Control Graph: select a commit, then a file
    History of one file (ep 10) the Timeline view in the Explorer
    Blame (ep 10) Git: Toggle Git Blame Editor Decoration in the Command Palette
    Compare with a branch or tag right-click a commit in the graph, then Compare with… (or Compare with Merge Base)
    Resolve a conflict (ep 9) Resolve in Merge Editor, then Complete Merge
    Stash and restore Git: Stash, Git: Pop Latest Stash in the Command Palette
    Cherry-pick (ep 13) right-click a commit in the graph, then Cherry Pick
    Give up on a merge, rebase or cherry-pick Git: Abort Merge / Abort Rebase / Abort Cherry Pick

    And the things that have no button, so you use the terminal: --fixup commits, interactive rebase and --autosquash, the reflog, bisect, range-diff, and --force-with-lease. (The GitLens extension adds an editor for interactive rebase and more, if you want a graphical version of those.)

    Things we only mentioned

    Stash. Real work gets interrupted. You’re halfway through an edit, and a colleague asks you to look at something on another branch. You can’t switch branches with half-finished changes in the way, and you don’t want to make a messy commit. Stash puts your uncommitted changes in a drawer and gives you a clean working directory:

    BASH 

    git stash push -m "README scratch note"     # put them away, with a label
git stash list                              # what's in the drawer?
git switch main                             # do the other thing...
git switch my-feature                       # ...and come back
git stash pop                               # take the changes out again

    OUTPUT 

    Saved working directory and index state On my-feature: README scratch note
stash@{0}: On my-feature: README scratch note

    Some variations: git stash push -u also stashes new, untracked files, git stash apply is like pop but keeps the stash in the drawer, and git stash drop throws one away. In VS Code, run Git: Stash (it asks for an optional message) and Git: Pop Latest Stash from the Command Palette. Git: Stash Staged stashes only what’s staged, which is git stash push --staged and needs Git 2.35 or newer.

    Worktrees. Sometimes you want two branches checked out at once, such as a release branch for a quick fix while your feature is in the middle of a change. Instead of stashing and switching, make a second folder for the same repository:

    BASH 

    git worktree add ../peakfinder-hotfix release/0.2

    You get a new folder with release/0.2 checked out. Work there, commit, and delete it when you’re finished (git worktree remove ../peakfinder-hotfix). VS Code can manage worktrees too.

    The merge base. The merge base of two branches is the commit where they diverged: git merge-base main my-feature. It’s what git range-diff and VS Code’s Compare with Merge Base compare against.

    Take-aways

    Nobody does all of this at once. Here are the habits we’ve covered, roughly in order of how much they give back:

    1. Plan the change, then the commits.
    2. Make commits atomic, with messages that say why.
    3. Use fixup for mistakes in earlier commits, and autosquash before you share.
    4. Rebase onto main rather than merging main into your branch. Push with --force-with-lease.
    5. Review your own branch first, then ask for review.
    6. Let CI check what a person shouldn’t have to.
    Challenge

    Challenge: your first step

    1. If you like, add an alias or two from the list above, and try them in your peakfinder clone. (Or skip this: it’s optional.)
    2. Decide one habit from the take-aways that you’ll try on your own work next week. Tell your partner, and say what might get in the way.

    Keep it small. One habit that you actually use is worth more than six that you don’t.

    There’s no single answer. A popular first choice is fixup and autosquash, because you can start with it today, on any branch, without anyone else changing what they do.

    If you’re not sure, try this on your next piece of work: write the commit plan first, make each commit one idea, and run git lg before you ask for review to check that it reads like a story.

    Where next

    • Pro Git, the free book, at git-scm.com/book. Chapters 3 (branching), 7 (tools) and 10 (internals) go deeper on everything here.
    • Learn Git Branching, an interactive game that draws the graphs as you type: learngitbranching.js.org.
    • Conventional Commits, if you want a commit message convention: conventionalcommits.org.
    • The reference page in this lesson has a cheat sheet of the commands and a glossary.
    • The extras page has a short guided peek inside .git (blobs, trees and packfiles), and reading on how git works, on branching models such as git flow, and on the topics in this workshop.

    Thank you

    We’d love to hear what worked and what didn’t.

    This episode is a menu. It’s fine to skip most of it, or to tell people it’s there to read afterwards. If you do one thing, do the take-aways and the “one habit” challenge.

    The challenge is also a quiet way to end. Ask two or three people to share their chosen habit.

    Before you finish: point people to the reference page, remind them their forks and branches are theirs to keep, and share the feedback link.

    Optional extras for a longer session or a follow-up: how git stores files (objects, trees, packfiles), git bisect with a script on a bigger history, git rerere in action, worktrees as an exercise, and a look at a real project’s pull requests.

    Key Points
    • Aliases and settings are personal choices: git’s defaults are fine, and you only need to change what’s bothering you
    • VS Code covers staging, amending, history, blame, conflicts, stash and cherry-pick. Fixup, interactive rebase, the reflog, bisect and range-diff need the terminal
    • Pick one habit to adopt first. Atomic commits and fixup with autosquash give the most for the least effort
